LADTES' LETTER

Mt Mum NELL/E, .In millinery, the lowecrowned felt hate, with spreading feathers, in modified " Trelawney " style, are rivalled by the wide, upturned toques, with high plumes, aigrettes, and fancy plumage, which are undoubtedly becoming to the generality of Englishwomen. Milliners do not appreciate the prediction as to a change of coiffure, since neither hats nor toques are wearable with low-dressed Lair.

Avery handsome black velvet hat is trimmed with bows of black velvet and long black ostrich leathers, up the stems of which runs a narrow row of black velvet, on which is threaded at intervals little paste buckles. A white chiffon scarf is attached to this, which has numerous rows of nar- row black ribbon velvet at the ends.

Felts are shown in all the pale grey, antelope, fawn, and almond tints, and felts of dark or solid colours are not used by the best houses, In black hats, drawn satin, velvet, and chenille are popular, but toques show a wondrous combination of straw and chenille, gold tinsel satin and chenille, or fancy straw, laden with large black sequins, the up- turned front especially being covered in this fashion. Dresses for girls of 11 to 16 are now usually made with belted bodices, and both braid and narrow ribbon velvet are especially favoured for trimmings. Wool poplin, serge, Melton cloth, and vigogne are the fashionable fabrics for general wear, as these stand wear and tear, and are yet smart when prettily made and trimmed. For school and country wear the coat and skirt is affected for growing girls, and here frieze, homespun and tweeds are more in request, as being ex- tremely durable and requiring less in the way of trimming.

For s young girl of 11 to 16 a delightful drees can be made in red vigogne, with black velvet bands and revers, small jet buttons, and the vest of red surs.h. A bright: blue is also effective with black vellet, or a dull r(ddish heliotrope with petunia velvet. The bodice opens down the front, and the 1.)-.c.k is attached to the skirt with three hooks ard eyes, •.he lining of the bodice forming a basqua down to Ili • I ips, and this goes under the skirt, and keep, t e waist neat and trim.

The blouse is std. beloved of E Iglishwornen, but . is now made with a fight ba..k and less fulness in front. Qaiis tight fitting bodices have fancy basques and tails 13,:hind, and the fronts either brought to one or two short points, or finished with folds of silk or velvet, timuJating a ceinture or fanciful Swiss belt. The pinarore style remains, but much modified, the over-part going much higher, leaving only a email yoke, and the fronts opening over a narrow plastron.

An exquisite blouse is made in pale mauve glac4 Bilk, tucked all over the upper part of the bodice, and also in groups on the sleeves. The corselet is of white glace silk, veiled with butter-coloured Cluny lace, which also appears on the revers, and the design is outlined with tiny frills of mauve satin ribbon. The vest is of accordion-pleated white chiffon, with a kilted jabot of the same edged with baby ribbbon, and similar frills trim the sleeves at the wrists and the back of the collar. Vests or plastrons are quite narrow, and even then narrowed in effect by waistcoat pieces of brighter colour or contrasting material, which lie partially over the plastron on either side. Thus, for instance, a bodice of the fag., onahle heather tint would have waistcoat pieces of bright helio- trope silk lying over a vest of tucked or corded primrose silk. Many tight-fitting bodices are made in this fashion, with banded waists, and showing no fulness, except in the tucked vest, which pouches ever so little over the centre clasp. Although the trimmed, fl'Ainced, draped, and tablier skirts are undoubtedly the fashion, plain skirts have by no means departed, and the majority of the cloth gowns shown tor the late autumn and early winter have plain skirts, made quite long, and with trimmings so arranged as to suggest a shaped flounce or a tablier put on separately. At the more advanced modistes very few plain skirts are seen, but many wheu on have quite the effect of a plain skirt, being made with separate under- skirt or foundation, which, to the validated, looks like a petticoat, and is only visible when the skirt is raised. plumage is indescri Fancy p bable, so many colours are intermixed, but pale-coloured feathers, wings, and tufts are now closely strewn with large chenille dots in place of the small fiat sequins, which be- came so very common. Chenille is the fashion of the moment, and entire toques are composed of a cenille lattice-work, mounted on colour, this re- appearing in the cachpeigne or front folds, and upheld by the inevitable buckle of paste, steel, or strasse. Your loving JENNIE.

div.head: "WOMEN'S CHAT."
div.p: "WOMEN'S CHAT."

The Duke of York during his last sad viiit to Copen- hagen was ab'e to do much toward he'ping to smooth out the difficulties which have aris.n lotween Princess Charles of Denmark aeid her Danish relalves. Toe Duke has always bad greit iofluence over Her Royal Flighn,•ss and to the great relief of the Prince and Princess of Wales,he has at length succeeded in reconciling Princess Charles somewbat,to her position as the wife of a second son. From their earliest days, the brother and sister have been devoted to each other, and a happier, gayer, or snore frolicsome pair, it would have been difficult to end.

At the last moment, when all arrangements had been made for the Princess to accompany her mother and brother to this country, and her apartments prepared at Sandringham, she decided to remain in Denmark, and travel later,arrivin4 in time to join the family party which will assemble about the end of the month, in honour of the Princess of Wales' birthday. On the first of Dezember, Her Royal Highness will have attained her My-fourth year, and in AI srch next wi I have held her title thirty-five years, a period which bias only been ex- ceeded by one of her predecessors, viz., Augusts, the daughter-in-law of George H. There are rumors to the effect that the betrnfhal of Princess Victoria of Wales will shortly be announced ; and that the close of the next London season will are her duly installed in her new home. The Princess has passed her thirtieth birthday, but she by no means looks her age .She is one of the mcst amiable of the Queen's granddaughters, and, if there is any truth in the present rumors, will be sorely missed by the Princess of Wales, whose coestant companion she has been since the marriage of Princess Charles of Denmark. _ .

_ The family arrangements of the Duke and Duchess Cumberland whom the aged King of Denmark has accompanied back to Gmunden for a lengthy stay, suit him well, as they are much on the same simple lines as he is accustomed to. The principal meals of the day, are a dinner at one o'clock, of the most substantial proportions, and at eight, supper, of a very simple description. Although our Queen's dinner is not served until nine o'clock, the banquet is always over by ten, the Royal meals being served with commendable rapidity. By eleven Her Majesty has taken leave of all gueits, who are then free to retire to the apartments prepared for them, or leave the Castle, as the case may he. Those who have been commended to " dine and sleep " depart next morning by an early train, not later than eleven, as silently as spirits. No formal farowell is accorded them.

At Mar borough House and Sandringham, the cuisine is almost entirely French, the Prices being a grvat lover of French dishes The Princs's chef is a man of no little import snce, and of course es rapport with all the celebrated art'ste of the kitchen in Europe and America. The menu is invariably couched in the French language, heed rarely being taken of the nationality ot guests. At all dinner parties where members of the Royal Family are present, finger glasses—which in a few great houses take the firm of golden dishes, kept specially for the purpose—are handed only to the Royal guests. This strange custom had, it is said, its origin in the days of the earlier Georges when the Jaeobitee were wont to play a curious trick upon their enterasiners. In r th os ee days no one would have dreamed of rising mth table without tossting their sovereign. Indeed the nmissian would have been imprudent, if not positively 'dangerous. When the toast of " The King" was given, those among the aristocracy who were still inclined to the cause of the Stuarts,made a practice of holding their glasses over the fiager bowls, to signify that they drank not to the reigning King, hut to the " King Over the water." Until the accession of the Quem, finger bowls ceased to be used in the Court.

The sodden return of the your'? Duke of Manchester from Australia was a great surprise to his mother and sister, a ho knew nothing of his coming until his arrival at Marseilles was announcrd. It appears that he is anxious to renew his engagement with Miss Joan Wit- son but la's relatives by no means approve, or ever did approve of the match, and are 'quoit anxious that the Duke shall not marry other than his cousin Lady Mary Douglas Hamilton. Lady Mary is only as yet in her fifteenth year, so in any case some time must elapse be- fore any engagement can be entered into. She is worth about £5,000 a year, and own Eacton Park, Brodick Castle, and other properties toth at home and abroad. Mrs. Alec Tweedie who wrote among other things that very entertaining book of travels 'S Through Finland in Carts," has in the press a life of her father the famous Dr. Harley which should be full of interest not only to the profession, but also to the general public. Mrs. Tweedie is a very handsome woman, and possesses the most charming macnerE. One of her pet hobbies is a novel collection of autognphs of famous men and women who havo dined at her house. She gets them to write their names in pencil upon the table slips, and these she afterwards embroiders in red flax thread. Good 'men being a thing that wears almost fee for ever, Mrs. Tweedi, a collection will doublets become more and more valuable in the course of time. _

- Nowadays titlen women writers are numerous indeed. Among the beet kPown perhaps are the Dueh.as of Sutherland, Lady Warwick, Lady Constance Howard, Lady Colin Ctmpbell, Lady Helen Craven, the Bon Mrs. Henniker, and Lady Jenne. The first woman in these Liles who managed t) live by her pen, was the notorious Afphra Behu.Cailterbury was the town usually given as ner birthplace, but quite lately her 'my:lama' regist-r has been discovered at Wye, which gives the date of her birth, biptism as July 10, le4o. _ .

, . Deep ail tinges ara much en evielenee both on day, and evening gewns.That the mode is a graceful one is be- yond doubt, but Only those blessed with a dberal allow- ahce should patronise it. Silk fringes arc not only costly, but they wear badly. So far tivy have appeare I chiefly • on 'cmwns cut in the polonaiss style, slightly draped on- the hips, and arranged over a petticoat of some other fabric. . .

Artis's and sculptors h-ive long groaned over the epau- lette aid puff, hat at the present tim- they have matter all their own was, and are ally to have for somo con- s;d,rable /time to come. The outline the nhnilder and ' arm is uninterrupted, and though just at first this has a meagre and even mean effect, we shall soon learn to pr ,fer it. The outline of the ncck too is new visible, This has been maltreated for several !els -,T) s. sometimes being ruined by projecting pieces of lace, silk or velvet, and sometimes by thick folds of velvet, which thickstied what shauld be delicate and slender, ' The appearance of some of the Christmas numbers, remind us of the appr Ach of the festive season, aud the Postmaster-General has issued a notice giving the latest date letters and cards should be posted for distant parts of the world en as to reach tlvir destination by Christmas, or New Y,ar's Day. The Duke of Norfelk has an eye for thesa small matters, as well as the more substamial reforms which have distinguished his re- gime at the Post Office. Be has certainly la,en a great success in his capacity as Postmoster-General,

The Duke of Norfolk is Earl Marshal, and Hereditary Marshal of England, a distinction conferred in 1872 on the sixth Duke and his heirs in pepetuity. As Earl Marshal the Duke has charge of the arrangements observed at state funerals, and he is empowerad in the prestnce and absence of the sovereign to tear a gold-n staff tipped at each end with black, with the upper part adorned with the Royal Arms and the lower with those of his own family. Th 3 Duke Lii4o ho'cla an annual grant of £2O, in connection with the office, payable to himself and his heirs for ever. The tendency of the public to neglect going to church Is often a subject of complaint. It is true it hal been the theme of countless homilies for hundreds and hundreds of years, but there is a general agreement that the falling off has been very marked in recent years. Elderly folks can recodect a different state of things, and the change is attributed to the excessive love of pleasure and amusement which distinguishes this genera- tion from its forerunners. Golf playing is now a regular thing en Sunday, and on all the high roads one sees a larger number than ever cycling, driving or upon some other pleasure bent. It is not perhaps that buns is nature has changed,but that pesple have more facilitiaa, and a greater variety of amusements and morearnoneY spend upon them. There is no sol ice ti Vie moralist in these reflections, but it is always best to see the facts clearly, and it must be admitted that attention to reli- gious duties has not kept pace with our advance in 50 many other fields in re cut years. Curried kidneys.—Take some sheen's kidneys, cut them in half skin, and stew them in a little brown ' gravy, nicely seasoned. Cook slowly, and when tender, cake them up, and thicken the gravy with a teaspoonful of flour and the same quantity of curry powder, madl into a paste with a little cold stock. Stir till it thickens, return the moat, and stand aside 30 minutes. Make a ring of bailed rice, place the curry in the centre, and serve. " MADGE."

THE EXAMINER _ FRIDAY, NOVEMBER 11 1898

and the arrows whirred through the air, our non- combatants moved under cover of the rocks. Our fire, deadly and incessant, paralysed many of the invaders; and as horseman after horseman fell to the ground, the riderless animals rushed through their ranks, causing confusion which must lead to defeat unless remedied at once. Mark now embraced his chance, and led the way down the rugged mountain side, picking the foe off by dozens, and inspiring confidence in the men of Golden Vale. This was strengthened when the Princess Olive ran on ahead and revealed herself. Thus she spake to the curious who crowded about her: „ _ _

"Men of Golden Vale, ye know Olive, Kana's daughter. I was rescued from torture and death by these white men who fight with you against my captors. Ere the invaders yonder rally, charge them with might. that they recover not. Otherwise they may conquer and lay waste our homes, killing - aged., making slaves of our younger men and Jeiling our women. If it be that ye lack courage, then I will lead to victory, or die with you! What mean ye, men of Golden Vale ? " The reply was practical, for with a great shout her people waved their standards, brandished their weapons, and rushed upon their foes, asking no quarter and giving none. Lest we should hit our friends we picked off the fugitive stragglers, and nearly every shot fired by us was a crisp messenger of death. In joining with Kana's people against Muro, we acted upon this principle—When there is a likelihood of being kicked, kick harder. Or, as a cannibal once put it to me: If you don't want to be gobbled, gobble. After a sharp but short contest Muro beat a hasty retreat, and the cheers of our party added to the zest of the conquerors in following up their victory by hot pursuit. Meanwhile our party had all descended to the valley. There is no doubt that our presence inspired Olive's friends with confidence at the crisis, for the appearance of Misro had struck superstitious awe into the breast of many an Indian defender. How- ever, the success of Olive's kinsmen ensured us a hearty welcome, and paved the way to a reception by Queen Kana which became the starting point of many vicissitudes in the blind resolve of Mark Pepys to carry out his daring object.

Latchford played hotter in the second half a d managed to reach the Cheatham circle, where they were awarded a corner. This proved of no advan- tage to them, Parker clearing awl, and the remainder of the game was spent in the visitors' circle, two More goalp bsing sidled for Cheetliam. The game ended in a win for the home team by six goals to nothing. The score would have bsen greater but for the efforts of the players to gain honours individually, although the pass- ing in the open was good. ALTRINCHAM V. STOCKTON HEATH, —played on Satur- day at Arpley. The home team made a good show until three parts of the game had been played when they fell away and Altrincham increased th-ir score from one goal to 4 goals. div.head: ACTION BY A WARRINGTON RUBBER COMPANY.
div.p: ACTION BY A WARRINGTON RUBBER COMPANY.

The case of the Warrington Rubber Works, Limited, V. the Amalgamated Pneumatic Tyre ComPany,Limited, on Monday came before the Court of Appeal on he appeal of the defendants from the crier of Mr. Justice Lawrance, dated August 9, 1998, affirming the order of Master Wilberforce referring the matter in dispute to an official referee. Mr. Germaine. counsel for the defend. ants (appellants) said the action was brought for the price ot goods supoli td and work and labour done. The defendants admitted the claim, but set up a counter- claim on the ground that. the contract was a contract of warrant to deal with the goods in a certain way, and this the plaintiffs had not done, and consequently part ot the goods sent to the defendants were valueless. They contended that they were entitled to set these off against the total amount calmed. The def(ndacts wished to have the counterclaim tried by a common jury—The appeal was dismissed with costs.

div.head: SECRET OF MARK PEPYS.
div.p: SECRET OF MARK PEPYS.
BY FRED J. PROCTOR,
Author of "Timothy Twill's Secret," "Jean
Marlou, " ``Dr. Dobbs," -- CHAPTER XIII. TEE INVASION OP GOLDEN VALE.

Now, this passage of the Royal caverns was of great antiquarian interest to us; but, to be honest, I must say the results were disappointing. There were no hieroglyphics on the walls, nor anything colossal or singular about the passages. The floor of the largest cavern was comparatively smooth, and covered with an impalpable dust that had accumu- lated through the course of years. "Follow precisely in my footprints," said Olive, "for danger lies hidden nearer the dead." The meaning of this strange caution was not apparent, but we implicitly followed her instruc- tions. At the further end of this cavern we were somewhat horrified to discover the dried remains of four savages. "What a ghastly sight!" I observed to Mark, who shrugged his shoulders as Olive held the lantern for us to get a clearer view of her ancestors. "No feet, save mine, have trodden within these sacred walls for years," said the girl, addressing Pecos, as we peered through the dingy air to examine the dead. They all sat, their arms crossed upon their breasts, knees approaching the chin, facing the east. Thus centuries ago the source of light inspired the barbarians with ideas of the resurrection. The mother and father were together, the son near the latter, the infant girl in a line with the others and near the mother. I noticed that the dead woman's fine dark brown hair was well preserved; the helix and anti-helix of her ears were not pierced like ordinary Indians' ears, but a piece of hollow reed was perfectly preserved in each lobe. The single perforation was not noticeable in the infant girl, whose delicate frame had been wrapped in deer- skin, remnants of which even now covered the cotton fabric used as a shroud. Twisted grasses, cotton, hair, and the bark of willows formed the simple warp and weft. It took us fully twenty minutes of cautious walk- ing to reach the entrance from Golden Vale. We cleared the loose stones, broke the cement, and at last crawled through an opening into the cunningly- devised coppice, right glad to get a breath of fresh air and see the early dawn breaking. To escape detection, Olive had blown out the light; and now she very cautiously led us by a narrow zigzag path round the dome of the moun- tain, where we obtained a good view of the Golden Vale defile, now being stoutly attacked and de- fended. As we stealthily approached nearer, the whoops and execrations became more spasmodic, and the musket shots few and far between.

"My people have held their ground," Olive explained, "and daylight will assist them in spying out the strength and position of the enemy." There was a lull in the battle, and we strained our eyes to catch a glimpse of the combatants. As the light increased we saw a special gathering of the invaders, as though they held a council of war. Then their marksmen spread right and left, for from ledges and from behind boulders and trees flashes issued. The men of Golden Vale met this with:guerilla warfare, and as their marksmen were more sure of the ground, shots sped from heights not far removed from where we hid. Several feints at retreat were made, to draw the bulk of the in- vaders between the embankments, but the subterfuge failed, proving that the assailants were led by someone who knew the sluices could be opened, and a large portion of the defile flooded. "Let us cower low," spake Olive softly, "lest the stray shots and arrows hit us." "Look!" whispered Mark; "Kana's warriors have dropped the defensive, and are pressing towards the entrances. They have estimated the enemy, and mean to defeat him without having ,recourse to the flooding." And then an idea flashed through his mind, for he seized Pecos by the arm and bid him inquire of Olive whether she could lead them secretly to any spot where our lads might attack the enemy's flank. "To do that," rejoined the girl, her eyes flashing in the rosy light at the thought of assisting her people, "we must return and wend our way round the southern side of the mountain. The path is not dangerous, and the cliffs command a view within easy shot of the foe. With my pass-word and assistance, we can descend." Decision was a trait in Mark's nature, and on this occasion it stood us in good stead; for when we joined our party already Lucia's excitable temperament had agitated them to a dangerous pitch. Their reassurance was none the less warm when they received the word to advance, for these wild spirits needed occupation to keep them out of mischief. Like the Athenians of old, they ever sought some new diversion. But the same thing applies all the world over, and at all times. If the people are provided with health-giving recreation, and mental enjoyment, they will not get into much mischief. Even Lucia's idle hands were prone to evil; and she was too piqued even to add a word of welcome. In this she betrayed the frailty of her nature, and though Mark said little, I after- wards learnt that her conduct on this occasion made a deep impression on him. "Sandy," he observed, "a quarrel with a foreign nation has saved many a country from civil war. We returned in the nick of time, or Lucia's rest- less disposition had infected the lot. I'll give them plenty of work; they shall not have time to backbite and brawl."

The object of our manceuvre put fresh life into Olive's movements, and our people were not laggards in the mission. As the roseate hues of the eastern sky tipped the crags and forest-crowned domes we stealthily crept along wooded gulleys and took up our positions behind projeOting rocks and mighty firs, waiting for the word of command. Through my glass I saw the soldiers of Golden Vale gathered in battle array behind a dense wood, and presently they cautiously filed from ambush and wormed their way through the defile to the remote entrance where the enemy challenged them. There was little firing now, the ammunition probably being reserved on both sides; so that in the event of a close encounter the Princess hoped the warriors of her tribe would maintain their courage and rout their foes. We crept onward by hazardous paths and watched the fray until the light waxed sufficiently strong for better observation. Then Lucia looked through ray telescope, and I noticed how hard she strove to suppress her agitation. The reason was shortly discovered.

_ We gazed intently upon the desultory fray for fully fifteen minutes, when Mark exclaimed: "See! they have come within spear-throw, and the invaders prepare to charge! Muro, the Castilian, leads against Olive's people! What do you think of that Lucia? " . _ 2

"I think your eyes deceive you," answered she, her face blanched and her lips quivering with excitement But Mark was again scanning the enemy. "From the west come scores of Muro's reserves —lndian horsemen well-armed. The brigand waves his sword as a welcome. We shall see hot work presently. Lads, look to the condition of your firearms; spread yourselves out to the best advan- tage, and when I say Fire!' let Muro's horde have it hot! Leave the rascal himself for me!"

Lucia approached him, extended her hand with fear and trembling, as though anxious to arrest his attention while she pleaded ; but the impulse passed, and sighing, she let the opportunity slip for ever. In like manner fortunes and battles have, been lost through fatal hesitancy. Yet, looking back after all these years, one is apt to think that in Lucia's case it was predestined so. Immediately upon the reinforcements joining Muro's men they formed up fully four thousand strong, little imagining that Kana's reserves were full of fight and waiting for the final charge. As this was about to start I was conscious that somebody among our party either maliciously betrayed us, or by a foolhardy act hDd revealed our presence, for as the foe formed in battle array, a small party of Muro's men were told off to ascertain our object and strength. This drove us to act on the offensive a little too soon, but it shewed the men of Golden Vale that white friends had unex- pectedly turned up. Mark gave the word "Fire!" and for a moment Muro's braves quivered. But the Castilian's voice was now heard above the din urging his men forward; and soon the serried ranks of Kana's warriors were steadily preparing to resist the onslaught. I looked round, and Lucia's hand was on her palpitating heart; there was a look of wild loveliness about her face; and when Mark paused a moment and 'glanced at her, his frown accentuated the bitterness of her feelings. Yet she met his gaze with wonderful composure, for his eyes glittered with the brightness of a tomahawk flashing in the moonlight. As the bullets whizzed

div.head: CHAPTER XIV. DORY RANA RECEIVED MARK.
div.p: CHAPTER XIV. DORY RANA RECEIVED MARK.

When Muro threw up the sponge his fleet horse alone saved his scalp, but the carnage among the retreating foe was fearful. The invaders had not anticipated the strength of Kana's warriors, nor the military skill possessed by her leaders. Like Boadicea of old, the Queen herself usually went forth to war, mounted upon a splendidly caparisoned charger. Not so much her fighting proclivities as her queenly presence and keen judgment, gave her the power she possessed over the soldiers. Our people remarked on the grace and charm of Olive when she cast aside the overalls provided by Lucia, end harangued the men. Then, as a dutiful d kngliter anxious to allay anxiety, she sought her Royal mother, her eyes glorious with expectancy, her long black hair reaching below her waist in two plaits, and her lithe figure draped in a white robe of fine cotton.

Not finding the Queen at once, Olive gave instruc- tions for our safe escort, and went to the palace for clothing suited to her rank. When she came forth the thin cotton dress she wore was spun to such a degree of fineness as to resemble velvet, while from the waist upward it resembled muslin. In various devices the delicate hair of animals and birds' feathers were interwoven, which made the cloth of considerable beauty, and upon her breast hung a richly-chased silver cross, resembling those I have met with carved in the temples of Lorillard city. The horizontal bar was studded with rubies, pearls, and diamonds ; the vertical bar was plainer, but a beautiful device of eagles' feathers and a swan-like figure crownod and sur- mounted it. This, Pecos informed us, betokened Olive's birth as a Royal Princess. None, save Kana's daughters, dare wear the cross. Unlike the Toltec maidens, her dress was drawn about her loins by a brilliantly-coloured silken girdle, and the leather straps which bound her sandals were studded with pretty beads and precious stones. At Mexican dances and bull-fights I afterwards saw amorous belles in gala attire ; I listened to the soft and pleasing cadence of an Indian sermon to native women who live a kind of quasi-seraglio life ; I held my glass for bewitching Mestizos to dip their rosy lips in it; but I never saw so beguiling a daughter of Eve as this girl of some eighteen summers.

........ The soldiers gave their fair Princess a hearty welcome, waving their spears, javelins, and clubs, thickly set with gold, silver, and steel nails. They tapped their metal shields, and as they stamped to the rythm of a war-song their tightly-fitting chain tunics jingled in strange combination of sound. Unlike the warriors' cumbrous head-dresses, as seen at Tula, Kana's ordinary soldiers simply wore a thick metal skull-cap lined inside with cloth, with metal flaps tied under their chins and the crown decorated with feathers. Each man wore the carved bone of the mountain sheep upon his breast, and the ordinary warrior's thick hair was ~it in the fashion set by the resthetic poets of the dramatic stage. The foot-soldiers were noble fellows, none less than five feet eight inches high, and many rising over six feet, while the shorter men of the tribe were chosen as archers and horse- men, or formed an ambulance corps. The com- manders and men of note wore costumes of rare beauty, richly-embroidered tunics, hats of gold studded with precious stones, armour of steel, silver, and even gold. "I never saw a finer set of soldiers," observed Mark, as we watched the female nurses and medicine men attending to the fallen. "I notice that some to whom drink is given are soon over- powered." "Those are the wounded beyond hope o' recovery," I explained, "an' are unable to lift the poisoned pill which ilka ane carries in case o' capture or threatened torture, or to escape a lingering or painful death on the battlefield. Look! that puir fellow o'er there is beckoning us. Per- haps he wishes to say something afore he dies. Ile s no' Golden Vale warrior. Pecos has gone wi' Olive to see the Queen. Come, lat's see what this man wants.—Strange that he should pick us oot. . . . Tie seems t' ken 's. . . . 3/tiro's band was a composite lot." Mark put his hand on my arm and said: "Beware! '
I winked, and held my pistol in readiness, for as we walked the blood-sodden grass and stepped .7er the slain it was necessary to be wary of the assassin's knife.

The Indian's life was ebbing. His glistening eye and pain-drawn face prophesied his speedy dis- solution. I loosened his martli—the broad band round his middle—and this seemed to relieve pain. "Oh, noble lord," he said, feebly extending his hand to my cornpanion, "Mark Pepys of San Leno, and Sandy Dees, his best man, harken to the voice of a dying Indian. Soon the vultures will make a meal of my body; let me, therefore, remove the yoke from my mind. Mark Pepys, the wolves prowl about thy lair, the mountain lion stalks after thee and thine, reptiles crawl about thy path to sting thee to death." "I wish the fellow would drop this fignrative bosh," I impatiently observed in an undertone to Mark, as the Indian fell back faint. "He looks like a sub-chief o' that blackguardly gang which gagged me near Yerba Buena." The dying man recovered sufficiently to say, specially addressing Mark, "Before my brain is clouded, and a film covers my eyes, give me thine ear, that I die not accursed. lam he who led the raid on Puke's Delight. Nay, shrink not from me ; rend me limb from limb, if I lie. Listen, even the repentance of an Indian can be sincere ; so, as taught by the white missionary of Yerba Buena, I would wash out my guilt. Let me confess my transgression. I hated Pecos with a bitter hatred, but the white man had done me ,u wrong." He gasped as we bent forward to catch each word. "My tribe was paid in brandy and tobacco for assisting at the robbery of your treasures."

"By whom?" I eagerly asked. "By the tavern-keeper, Harry Puke." Mark started with surprise, and cried: "Non- sense; he was found tied down in his own cellar, and tied in such a manner that it was impossible for him to make the knots himself." "True," answered the Indian hoarsely, his face drawn and his eyes bloodshot, "and. I, at his request, tied the cords wherewith to deceive you." "The treasures," observed Mark, "were shipped by Muro's schooner that lay in the offing." "My lord, of their going I am ignorant." The Indian's life-blood was well-nigh spent. "Trust no woman with a secret," he whispered, "for either she will pine away in keeping it, or betray thee. My lord loves Lucia Diaz. She is a puma— her beauty and grace must be admired at a safe distance. There is danger in making a pet of her." Hemorrhage set in, and the Man added, with gasp: "Beware of Muro--" Glancing just then at Mark I noticed that ‘a horrible suspicion crossed his mind, but he stifled it. I bathed the Indian's temples, but

tieyond a few inutterin.'s ne saiu notaing runner that was intelligible. In a few minutes the end came, and when I closed the dead man's eyes, we examined his clothes and weapons. He had neither my missing telescope nor knife, but upon the third finger of his right hand was the very ring I wore on the heights to the north of the Golden Gate. "This savage," quoth I, "spoke the truth." "God help that knave, Muro," observed Mark,' grinding his teeth, "if ever he comes within arm's length or musket shot. I will kill him with as little compunction as I would a mole, and nail his dead body to a tree as a warning. The words of this dead man will ring in my ears for many a long day. Sandy, not a whisper to a soul, mind, on your honour. "Strictly on the square," I answered, as he grip my hand. ""e must wait patiently and watch. Yet," he added dubiously, "the fellow was non, compos mantis. The ring may have been given to him. His statement about Harry Puke was so mon- strously absurd 'that no sane man would believe it. "Why not ? " I urged, and he shrugged his shoulders. "By the way, Mark, did ye ken Puke afore ye arrived i' California? " "Sandy," he replied firmly but sorrowfully, "you are my friend. Now there are episodes in every man's life he wishes to forget. You will oblige me by not referring again to the home-country. If you do I shall ruffle your feathers with an evasive reply, or give you the cold shoulder when officers chip out the men get demoralised. know it is no good to lie to you with a glib tongue, for you , are so voluble that I should put my fingers in my ears in despair. This much, how- ever, I will say: I never intend to go back to reap my crop of wild oats. Sufficient for my day is du+ remembrance thereof; so for ever banish an unpleasant subject. . . . But about this red fellow's covert reference to Lucia's cunning—l can't make it out." I whistled, and my eyebrows said "How d'ye do ? " to my red hair, which so aggravated Mark that I wonder he had not knocked me down. But he looked at me contemptuously and lit his pipe. An uncomfortable pause ensued, during which we moodily strolled towards the city. Presently Mark brightened, as though anchoring his hope uPon some newly-discovered fact. "The Indian charac- ter," said he, "is always suspicious of white people, and I don't believe that Puke was maliciously disposed. In fact, I won't believe it, and that fellow was a blackguard for saying Fil)" You really can't rely on a quarter of the tales Yon hear about anyone. And it's a bit rough, when one is fond of a girl, to have even a suspicion of her fidelity dinned into your ears, That Indian has upset me. Here comes a royal pageant. Olive has evidently explained her absence, and no doubt sung our praises. Let us step out." The serried ranks of warriors, with .Queen Sans riding under a panoply, and Olive and Pecos W. ing . the way, now riveted the attention of our people. Towards us came Lucia, having left her serving-women, who were descending the hazardous slopes of the sacred mountain. The Senorita stared with astonishment at the splendour surrounding Rana, and at the richness of the Queen's dress and the dignity of her commanding figure. About her were nobles in flowing and handsome robes, feudatory lords, and other distinguished personages whom we afterwards discovered to be Knights of the Tiger, Lion,- and Eagle Orders, each class in a distinctive dress. These reminded me very much of the sub-divisions of the old Toltec Order, Tecuhtlis—for Kana's people were mild, affectionate, and aristocratic beyond any native race which crossed my path. Now, the Queen was decidedly Indian, but a fair woman with a clean complexion; handsome as the celebrated Tehuanntepec matrons; dignified, richly dressed, and cast in noble proportions. A idpa/ embroidered with gold and silver covered the back portion of her hair and fell in graceful folds down her back. A long silken robe draped with classic skill was drawn in at the waist by a sash similar to that worn by Olive; and her small feet were encased in dainty shoes. Ver neck, arms, and ankles were bare, and she had passed about thirty - seven summers. To her filigree necklace of beaten gold inlaid with precious stones hung a cross similar to that worn by her daughter, but of the more precious metal. Rings were upon her fingers, and she carried a hunting whip, the haft of ebony inlaid with silver. A slim, dark-eyed youth of delicate beauty led her fine white horse—a noble animal which pranced at Jip and threatened to knock Pecos down.

Mark admired all this magnificence, saying: "It is a grand spectacle! A large number of the soldiers are well-equipped with modern rifles, but the company of archers appear the most primitive of the army." _

The cavalcade' which consisted of fully twenty thousand souls, halted upon a hill; and one could see by their unstained bodies that this was the reserve army. The Queen dismounted, while Olive came forward with stately pride and saluted us. She made a graceful bow—such as no lady at Queen Victoria's levee could hope to beat—kissed her hands to the skies, touched her forehead and the ground with her Sniall tapering fingers, and advancing again about six paces, said in a silvery voice: "My lord, in the name of Queen Karns, I bid thee welcome to Golden Vale. As peace is thy message, let friendship be our bond." Thereupon Olive turned to her mother, extended her arms as a swimmer starting an even chest stroke, and again bowed. Then Kana raised her right hand with the two forefingers pointing upward, and the mighty host accepted the sign as a token of goodwill towardii us. The huzzas were deafening, but far more shrill and nasal than British cheers.

"The Queen," said .Pecos, addressing Mark, "having heard from her daughter, of thine assis- tance in her rescue, and moreover having seen for herself thy friendly help against the vanquished horde, wishes to speak with thee. I pray thee, hasten to obey her command, so shall it fare well with thee and thine." Olive comprehended our hesitancy—especially when Lucia's face wore an expression of mingled jealousy and alarm—and approaching swiftly, took Mark by the hand and led him forward. The noble fellow blushed and smiled at Lucia, who was glanc- ing at him from the corner of her eyes, and no doubt wondering why she was not included in the presentation. The welcome was equal to the pretty sight, rendered more picturesque in the richness of light whiclh chased away the early morning dews. After a dignified bow, Kana's rich, clear voice was heard saying: "Welcome, my lord, to thee and thy trusty men. For thy rescue of Princess Olive our hearts beat in grateful acknowledgment. Olive wandered, not thinkng of the danger, and was seized as a lamb by the wolves. She was captive and panted for home, and our foes mocked her yearning. Then as a hand plucks the precious scroll from destruction, thou didet save the daughter of our royal house from certain death. Therefore, my lord, our hospitality share—the best of Golden Vale be thine, now and for evermore."

Mark, having heard this translated, bowed in stately fashion. Then Olive took Pecos by the hand, saying: "Listen, 0 Queen; thou hast heard the part taken by Pecos; how he risked his life to remove my bonds. I therefore ask for him such an estate in Golden Vale and such favour of the people as none shall envy when they know his good nature."
"In due course," answered the Queen, smiling, "Pecos shall have his reward." -

-4-Thanks, 0 Queen," responded the faithful hunchback. "I am the servant of the White Chief. Whither he goes, I go; for to him I owe my life and prosperity. Still, royal lady, I value thine interest, which is far beyond the reward of my service and duty to the Princess. Long live Queen Kana. I have spoken." This peculiar and chivalrous response ended, Lucia was presented by Mark with every expression of good feeling, Kana kissing the Senorita's fore- head, and Olive striving to please her new friend. Meanwhile the Indian doctors 'and nurses were busy among the wounded, and their medical shill testified to a profound study of the healing art, though they were very jealous of prying eyes, that their enemies might not obtain a knowledge of their essences and compounds. One nauseous and very bitter medicine left a persistent and disagree- able after-flavour, but its effect upon the human system was immediate and exhilarating, giving physical power and mental activity apparently without any detrimental reaction. It produced happy contentment and sleep, and was a declared antidote • for poison. The tincture was obtained from a species of the cactus plant about the size m a walnut, which grew in places difficult of access upon the rock soil of Golden Vale, and was prized as sacred. To obtain personal experience, I after- wards swallowed three small buttons which had been steeped in a kind e pid44, and without losing control of ray- senses the visions I saw of colour and landscape were ecstatic and wonderful. I must own to a very slight depression when after five hours the effects wore -off; but in the case of wounded Indians a teaspoonful of the cacti', tincture induced a condition of mind and body which greatly assisted recovery. The ambulance party brought forward numerous

div.head: AN ODD EXPLANATION.
div.p: AN ODD EXPLANATION.

carruages similar to those used by Montezuma IL in his Huaxateca expedition. These had been utilised for carrying spare spears and other war implements, or served as ambuscades along the excellent roads leading to the city. They welt larger but lighter than the Roman war chariots, and were mostly drawn by Indians, though white horses drew the royal chariot—an expensive and artistic affair of pine covered with brass all° studded with devices of silver and precious stones, somewhat resembling those ancient carriages I afterwards helped to unearth at Tula. The ceremony of welcome ended, Olive gall Mark, Lucia, and me a silver miniature charin carved like Pecos's bone, and a string of horsehair interwoven with silver threads, accompanied with rNuest that each should wear this token of fealt74 Kana's tender disposition led her among the sick warriors, comforting and soothing them as only good woman can. Furthermore, the Queen acted mercifully to those prisoners who desired< her clemency, and when the wounded were received the hospitals the feudatory lords, military nobles, and whole array of fighting men formed ° triumphal procession and marched eastward int° the city, where such things came to pass as rt° human being could possibly anticipate. We were allotted excellent quarters within the royal boundaries, and after the usual official courtesies, we were allowed that honoured freedom which liana's hospitable race knew so well how to bestow. What, with junketing and presents our people had a rare time of enjoyment, both the Princess and Lucia entering into this with spirit. Bat if ever the horrible fascination of a treacheroue resolution made a man suffer inexplicable anguish, that man was Mark Pepys. Although before me° he carried himself with dignity and composure., jet his mind was racked by a disturbing problem, and the more we were feasted the more unutterable his disgust. His own unnatural hypocrisy and pretence steeped a disagreeable task in gall, and he turned sick at the sight of his own brewing. Where lay the stolen treasure? By what consummate skill could he come •at it? Was it the part of an honourable English gentleman to kiss the hand bq would fetter? He pictured the meanness of betraying the confidence of such an heroic Queen; and I think the utter weariness and fatigue he experiencei after the exclusive royal feasts, made him hate the dal that gave birth to his miserable resolve. (To be continued.)

div.p: WIRKINGTON TOWN
00UNCIL.
ELECTION OF MAYOR.

A meeting of the Council was held at the Town Hall, Warrington, on Wednesday at noon, f,r the t urpose of electing a Mayor and other buf:in-Es. At the outset the Mayor presided. There were ali•o present rman Fairciough (deputy Mayor), aldermen Franccmo, Roberts, Sutton, Blackhurst, Hutchinson, and Bolton ; Councillors Heaton, Cannel!, Plumpton, SmethurA, Monks, Shillcock, Balton, Jolley, Tinnion, Grace, Urns. field, Longton, Bennat, Eltisen, Bari, Duncan, Peacocks, Shaw Grf eo, James Evans, F. R. Rolvits„ John Lee, and John Roberts, with Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk). Mr. Stanley Wilson (deputy town cleik), Mr. J. Fairhurst (norough trelsurer), Mr. T. Longdin (horough surveycr), Mr. Sutcliffe (asbistant surveyor). Mr. Bess (sanitary engineer), Dr. Gornall (medical offider of health), Mr. Luke Talbot (chief Con- stable), Mr. G. F. F. White (deputy magistrate's clerk), and Mr. C. Madeley (librarian). There was also a large attendance of thc: general public including Mr. T. B. Malkin.

THE RECENT ELECTIONS. The Tows CLERK read the names if the successful candidates at the recent enunicipil e e ELECTION OF MAYOR. The Meson said the next business was the election of Mayor for the ensuing year. His Worship then left the room, and the Deputy Mayor was voted to the chair Pro tern, on the motion of Alderman Surroer, seconded ley Aldei man BLACKHURST. Councillor SMETHURST said he regarded it as an honour which be did not expect to have to perform, to propese the re-election of Alderman John Edward Wright as Mayor ot Warrington for the ensuine year. It was an understood thing, evideetly, that the proposer and se- sender of the Mayor at the caucus meeting of the Ceun- eil should perform that duty also at the annuli meeting of the Council, and it afforded him much pleasure to do so. The duty. in a town like Warrington, was an im- portant one, and if he could not express himself with as much fluency and with as much eloquence as some ot the other members could, none could do so with great-r sincerity than himself. (Hear, hear.) Every member of the Council and every other burgess would express gratification at the step which was being taken that day,and they would also be pleased to know that Alder- man Wright had recovered from his recent severe illness. (Hear, hear.) A wcek or two ago they had almost given up hope witn regard to him, and they were, therefore, all the more pleased to see his genial c uetsnance in the chair. His conduct had given as ni...ch ,satisfaction in the town as the conduct of his predecessors had done, and he had, therefore, pleasure in proposing hie re-elec- tion. (Arpleuse•) Alderman ROBERTS said as lie seconded the resolution at the caucus meeting he had pleasure now in again prrformicg that duty. As they knew the duths or the ' office were so onerous that it was absolutely imperative that the health of the May or should be good to enable him to do his duty satisfactorily to himself and in the interests of the town. They hoped that so far as his health and comfort were concerned that the next year would be the best year of his life. (Applause.) Alderman SUTTON supported the motion befere the meeting, and said he did so because he felt that Alder- man Wright had discharged the duties of the office to the satisfaction not only of the members of the Council but of the ratepayers generally. He congratulated Alderman Wright on havieg suflicently recovered from his indisposition to accept office tor another year, and they could as members of the Council promise to render him all the assistaace that lay ia their power. (Ap- plause.) The motion was unan:mouslv and heartily agreed to. The Mayor shortly afterwarde re-mtere:i the room, wearing his chain and robs of office, and accompanied by the Depute Mayor, his proposer and seconder, aud the Town Clerk.

The Mason, who was cordially received thanked the members most sincerely for their renewal of confidence. When he accepted the office of Mayor twelve months ago he did so with some misgivings for fear that he might not fill the office with satisfaction to himself and to the Council, eepecially when he thought of the many eX- cellent men who hod preceded him. However, thanks to the loyalty and courtesy he had received at their hands, the year had been an exceedinzlv pleasant one. At the first public function, that of attending divine service, as most of them would remember be had a most anxious two bourn of it, during which time a son was born. (Laughter). He was now considered the hand- somest and best child in the kingdom—at least, his mother said so. It they doubted it they must argue it out with her. (Renewe(l laughter.) Early in the year he had the honour of opening the first trades exhibitioa of any importance that had ever been held in the town. This, as they knew, vi as a great success, both finan- cially and otherwise. Unfortunately, they did not share the financial part. He would net weary them by naming all the other matters that had claimed their attention during the year, but he must say one word about the magnificent art exhibition that they cloeeel the municir at year with.He doebted if any town in Great Britain of their size had had such a ehoice display of pictures. He thought that not only the Gorporation bur the whole town owed a debt of gratitude to various gentle- men for lending such valuable works ; and although they never expected an exhibition like that to pay its way, he considered the mousy exc..edingly well spent. (App‘auee). And now., just a word or two, in conclu- sion, as to the coming year. There was much to be done, and he hoped they would agree with him that they must face the work boldly and promptly. He was happy to think that them dear old town was uever more proeperous that it was to-dey, and if they worked with one mind, as it were, to do all in their Dower for the hest interest and prosperity of their dear old town they would live to rejoice that they were members of the Council. THE DEPUTY-MAYOR AND CHAPLAIN. The MLYO2 re-appointed Alderman Jamie; Fairclough , as deputy-mayor for rhe ensuing year. The Rev. Canon hei re-appointed as his chaplain.

, - THE LATE MR. JOHN BURGESS, J.P. The MAYOR said before proceeding with the further business of the meeting, he desired to refer to the death of Mr. Jobs Burgess. He knew (f no one who had played a more important part in the affairs of the town, and much that he did was for the gocd of the inhabi- tants. He devoted a life's service, and they could not question big motives in doing what he did. If only to refer to the sanitary improvements in the town which Mr. Burgees teok in hand many years ego, they owed him a great debt cot gratitude for the c'eanlier and healthier conditions in which they now lived. Mr. Bu,gess had filled, he might say, every pub- lic office. He was first appointed a member of the Coun- cil in 1850, and elected an alderman in 1859. He filled the offioe of Mayor for two years,from 1860 to 1862,and and retired alter 36 years' service in 1892. Mr. Burgess was made a magiatrate in 1880, and last year the Coun- cil thought fit to bestow upon him the highest honour they had in their disposal by making him a freeman of thelYrough, an honour he (the Mayor) was sorry Mr. Burgess had not lived long to enjoy. (Ap- plause.) He should be glad if as many members as could make it convenient venuld accompany him at the funeral and pay a last tribute to his memory. He concluded by moving the following resolution :—" That this Council receives with deem regret the announeement of the death of „John Bureees,Esq ,a Justice of the Peace and a Freeman of the Borough, and who twice held the office of Meyer, and to exorese ite high anpreciation of the long and valuable public services rendered by him to the Borough ; and that the Town Clerk be requested to convey to Mr.;. Burgess and her family its heartfelt ez. preision of sympathy with them in their bereavement. Atdrrnsn RLACKBORST 110Cand Alderman ROBERTS said he would like to sty a word or two in support of the resolution. fie had been aese- ciated with the late Mr. Burgesa for 26 years. It was Mr. Burgess who seconded his ;(411derman doberts'e) appointment 26 years ago to an important office, the acceptance of which brought him into constant contact with Mr. Burgess. Wnen he (Alderman Roberts) was elected a member of the Council he became a member of the Flealth Committee over which Mr. Bergesa pre- sided. and he was bound to say that no man with whore he had been acquaints d impressed him so favourably with a strengela of character and determination to do what he believed to be right in the intereste of the town as did Mr. Burgess. Those qualifications had laid Warrington—net only of to-day but of Lie future— under a lasting debt of obligation. He denigeed sani- tary reotains which had made Warrington so much better a place to live in than 30 years ago. Mr. Burgess in his pubic career sever ceneidered his business or privets ertgagemente—witn him the interests of the town came firet. Ho was sure the members of the Council rerretted that his latest years had been clouded by circumstances which he could not helpover which he had no cmtrol. (Hear, hear).

Ald”rman SUTTON sail ror over tw.rity years he sat with the late Mr. Burgess on several committ-e3, and for a number of years acted as deputy-chairman of the Health and Saritary C)mmittet of which ho was the chairman. No man since the incorporation of the Borough pail more attention t 3 his duties on the Counci or woress harder for the benefit of the inhabitants of Warrington than the late alderman Burgess did. His whole heart was in the work and no man made a greater personal sacrifice for the public service than he. (Hear, bear.) Councillor MONKS said as he was Mr. Burgess's suc- cessor as Chairman of the Sanitary Wmke; Committee it was necessary that he should say a little, hut Alderman Reterts had anticipate.] him in what he intanded to say. He (Councillor Monks) looked upon Mr. Burgess's con- nsction with public affairs in his capacity of Chairman of the Sanitary Works Commitco.. Whatever might he thought of Mr. Burgess's opinions, that was not the time nor the place to analyse them. (Hear, hear.) They could not but admire the persevernme and conscientious manner in whica h 3 stuck to him opinions, and forced them through in spite 0, all opposition. Most people would now admit that in many things Mr. Burgess was right and perfectly justi- gal in what he dd. The satisfactory state of the town at the present time was mainly due to his energy and perSiStellte iu pUgling for wara tae reforms which Were.
An Honest Man's Words.

Mr. Thomas Gladman, 12, Finnis' Court, Dover, a fine specimen of British working manhood told his own experience to a Newspaper reporter, who took down his words. Mr. Gladman, it will be seen, had a stroke of paralysis, and his case was pronounced " hopeless "on the best medical authority. He was per- manently and entirely cured by Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People. "I am," said he, "a nay vy, and thirty-nine years of age. On the 29th October last year I was getting out foundations for a sea wall at Dover. My work necessitated standing in the water. Early in the morning a strange feeling came over me— helplessness. I could not grip anything thoroughly. I left work and went home to bed, shaking from head to foot; for I had entirely lost the use of my right leg. I remained in bed, and. for four weeks only got worse. My heart was so much affected that I had to sit up in bed, and I had a terrible struggle to get my breath. "Doctors were called in, but they could not give me any hopes; I was paralysed from head to foot. On the last day of November, 1897, I was taken to the hos- pital, but gradually got worse, for I lost the sense of feeling all down the arm and leg. In January the doctors told me there was no possible hope; they said they had done all they could for me, and I should always remain as I was then. "Then ray ganger's wife asked if I would take Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People if she bought them for me. I consented, and started taking them. I had got into the second box when I began to notice a sense of feeling in the right leg. Friends got me up and dressed me, and I shuffled downstairs. From then I gradually improved. I walked with a stick until a few weeks ago, but I can now walk without it, and go a good distance, often walking 12 miles in the day." "Have you any doubt about your cure being effected by Dr. Williams' Pink Pills alone P" Mr. Gladraan was asked. "Not the slightest," he said. "Before I took them I had given up all hope. Exactly from, that time I began to get better." Mr. Gladman, who is a member of the Sons of the Phcenix Society, went on te state that he had started work again, being engaged on the groynes between Folkestone and Dover. "I can now," he said, "do hard, manual labour. I am doing tide work, with pick and shovel and bar, and am on my feet eighteen out of the twenty-four hours."

The cures reported k the newspapers from the use of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, include many thousands of cases of anmmia, general weak- ness, loss of appetite, palpitation of the heart, shortness of breath, early decay, all forms of female weakness, hysteria, paralysis, locomotor ataxy, rheumatism, sciatica, scrofula, rickets, chronic erysipelas, consumption of the bowels and lungs. They are genuine only with the full name, Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, and are sold by Dr. Williams' Medicine Company, 46, Holborn-viaduct, London, E.C., at zs. 9d. a box, or six boxes for 13$. 9d., post free. The genuine Pills are not a Purgative, and contain nothing that could injure the most delicate.

were on that committee. Ile ventured to think that he had done some good work on the varioua committees and he thought he should be reconenised in some way by being placed on the General Purposes Committee. He did net think any member of the Council would say that be had been fairly treiated. Councillor MONKS said he could not help giving ex- pressiun to his feelings at the course the discussion had taken. It seemed to be considered that his action with reference to the General Purposes Committee was taken from a personal point of view. Thee was the last thing he had in his mind. The General Purposes Committee ought to be an advisory committee and he was inclined rather to restrict it in numbers than to enlarge it. That was why he proposed to reduce it to 18 members. If the committee could not be restricted ne would prefer to let the matter stand, and he proposed to vote against the pressnt amendment. Councillor CROSFIELD thought a General Purposes ' Committee composed of the whole of the members of the Council would be quite unworkable. He believed it was tried some years ago. Tne MAYOR It hell been tried for two years and proved unworkable. Councillor Lee-wrote said he should vote against the amendment. The MAyoR said he had no feeling in the matter, but the scheme suggested had been tried and found to be al failure. It was impossible to get a good attendance. , Alderman Ronsers said he bad no recollection of the experiment being tried, but he had always been told that it had been tried and considered a failure. Many things had altered since then and it might be worth while to try it as an experiment. On that ground he should vote for the amendment. He wanted it to be clearly understood that 'there a;A a vary erroneous knowledge in the minds of many members of the Coun- cil as to what the General Purp isee Committee did. It , wag not true that what the sub-committees decided upon came before the Council as the general policy of the Council but he would remind them that the principal amount of the work—the most serious amount—was done by the sub-committees and would still have to be done by hem. There was a Parliamentary sub-coin-1 mittee and it would be impossible to carry on the Par- liamuntary work if everything in connection with it had to be submitted to the whole Council before it could be carried out. If there Was a distinct understanding that the sub-committees should be inaintaioed and not matte tors big he was in favour of the whole Council sitting on the General Purposes Committee. Ho knew there had lesen some feeling amongst members of the Council with reference to the General Purposes Committee. He(Alder- , mon Roberts) had to wait quite as long as many of them bef ore he became a member of that committee. In order ' to get over this feeling which he knew existed and which had excluded some of the best members of the Council from the committee, and bearing in mind what he had said with reference to the sub-committees be should vote for the amendment. Alderman BOLTON spoke in favour of the amendment. Alderman SUTTON explained that he objected to any alteration. There were 22 mambe.ra on the General Purposes Committee, and it was large enough. Councillor Sitew GREEN said if the whole Council composed the General Purposes Committee they would simply have to 4ppoint certain sub-committees. He did not see that it would be of any benefit at all. Councillor BurtTox remarked that under the present System there were many members who knew nothing of what wae goingon. He thought they all had a right to know.and was in favour of the amendment. Councillor lons Roamers thought the Council might try it as an experiment for twelve months. Councillor iiKA.TON felt ceitain that if it were given a twelve months' trial tney would find there was a diffi- culty in getting the members at the meetings. A vote was then taken. For the amendment there noted : Aldermen Roberts, Bolton, Hutchinson ; Coun- cillors Plumpton. Ellison, Duncan, Burton, James Evans Baird, Minion, F. R. Roberts, Peacock, Grace, Jolley, John Roberts, Heaton (16). Against : The Mayor, Alderman Francomb, Fairelough, Sutton. Bleckhurst, Councillore Shillccck, Monks, Bennett, Longtoa, Smethurst. Croifield, Lee (12). The m,,,yoe The amendment is c irritd by 16 votes to 12. (Applause). The Me vou It is nothing to get excited about. RETURNING OFFICERS.

Councillor &taw GREEN moved that the retiring officers be as follows : Town Hall, Alderman Roberts ; Whltecrlas. Alderman Hutchinson ; Bewsey, Alderman Fairclough ; Orford, Alderman Harrison ; St. John's Alderman Sutton : Fairfield, Alderman Wright; Howley, Alderman Francomb ; St. Austin's, Alderman Black- truest ; Latcnfotd, Alderman Bolton. Councillor SMETHURST seconded, and the resolution was carried unanimously. THE MAYOR'S INVITATION TO CHURCH. The MAYOR notified to the Council that it was his intention to attend divine service at the Parish Church on Sunday, and he would be pleased to have the com- pany of the Council, se many of his fellow to wnsmin who cared to come and also tie members of the Board of Guardians. (Hear, hear). Captain Waring had asked permiision for the Ambulance Corps to be present and they would Le in attendance. The Council then rose.

They all deeply deplored that the la,t years of his life should not have been lived under happier circumstances, and till, could now only exor,ss their regret and sympathy with the members of his family. (Applause). The resolution was unaninaouslv ,carried. ELECTION OF ALDERMEN.

Tha next business was the election of four aldermen to supply the places of th)se who went out of office on the 9th day of November. Thp rething aldermen were : Messrs. G. Blackburst, James Fairclough, Joseph Flarri- son and Thomas 11. Sutton. These gentlemea having retired from the room.

The MAYOR asked for the voting papers to be handed to him personally by the memb,rs of the Council. It wss found that every member had vote] for the retiring aldermen and they were therefore unanitnously re- elected.

The four aldermen having re-entered the room, the MAYOR said he had great pleasure in informing them that they had, been unanimously re-elected aldermen for the ensuing six peen. He hmed they would be spared for many long years to come to devote their time to the public service and that they might have t e honour of I being reelected again. (Applause.) Alderman BLAOITMURST thanked the Council for the honour conferred upon him. If God spared his lualth and life he h,ped he should be able to attend to his duties as well as he had done during the last six years. (Applause.) Alderman SUTTON said he supposed he must also thank the Council for electing him to arduous and responsible duties for the next six years. He hoped it would be at the same remuneration. (Laughter.) Some people thought that every alderman ought to seek re-election by the ratepayers. '(Hear, hear.) He had smee hard fights in the ward he represented ard he did not think he should object to have another good tussle in any of the wards. (Laugh- ter.) His friend Alderman Roberts had thrown out a suggestion that if he liked to resign he (Alderman Roberts) would also do so and conteA any ward in th borough with him. (Laughter.) He did no; know whether Alderman Roberts was joking--- Councillor Tr/germ Both of you have more sense. (Laughter). Alderman SUTTON : Alderman Rdb Irts said he was 1 I serious. (Laughter.) He (Aid, man Sutton) could only I 'say that he did not accept the challenge tvicause ho should have bsen very sorry to lasire left Alderman Roberts outside the Council. (Laughter.) Such an event would deprive them of any chance of an occa- sional tug of war and the pleasure which it gave them. (Laughter.) He thanked the members for the honour again conferred upon him. Alderman FAIRCLOUGH returned his sincere thanks to! the Council for again cleating him an alderman. He! would try in future to do his duty, and perhaps behave himself better than he had done. (Laughter and ap- plause.) _

div.head: MARRIAGE OF Mit. C. JACKSON
div.p: MARRIAGE OF Mit. C. JACKSON
11.0LMES.

At the Friends Meeting House, Manchester, last Thursday, the marriage was solemnised according to the usage of the Society of Friends of Mr. C Jackson Holmes, son of ex-Alderman Holmes, of Great Sankey, Warrington, to Miss Mary Elizabeth Sutton, eldest daughter of Mr. Edward Sutton, of Seymour-road, Cheetham Hill, Manchester. The bride's dress was slate and white silk with hat to match. There were no bridesmaids or best man. According to the custom of the society the bride- groom took the hand of the bride and declared as follows :—" I take this my Friend Mary Elizabeth Sutton to be my wife promising through Divine ' assistance to be unto her a loving and faithful hus- band until it shall please the Lord by death to separate us." The bride made a similar declaration, and then the marriage certificate was signed, the signatures being witnessed by some of those pre- sent, who also signed their names. The certificate was then read aloud by the Registrar and the cere- mony was complete, except that the register was signed after the close of the meeting. There is no such person as an"officiating minister." Anyone is at liberty to speak if he or she feels it right to do so, but no one is obliged—the parties marry them- selves. _ _

Ab the conclusion of the ceremony a reception was held at the Friends' Institute, Mount-street, Manchester, where a large number of guests assem- bled. The newly married couple afterwards de- parted for Leamington and district where the honeymoon is being spent. Deceased jumped from the bticony outside the ball-oom, and was instantaneously killed, A verdict of " Suicide :during temporary insanity' was returned. The solicitor acting on behalf the young man D'Arcy, sen- tenced to death for murdering another young man by stabb- ing him in Oakley-street. Lambeth, on Saturday morning received an intimation from the home secretary announcing that the Queen had commuted the Sentence to penal servi- tude for life.

Information has now been received regarding the confliet between the French and the Boubouris on the Ivory Coast. Two Europeans, who had gone up country for trading pur- poses. were killed by the Boubouris, and a French punitive expedition. while attacking the chief town of the tribe, was repulsed with considerable loss. The natives have now sued for peace. Further fighting has recently occurred in Uganda, the 27th Bombay Infantry, the Uganda hides, and Swahilis having been on different occasions attacked by Langos and Sou- &nese. the latter assisted by Waganda and Wangoro tribes- men, The attacks were beaten off the total British loss being 7 kille4 and 23 wounded.
