Tuz naval preparations,which Europe and still go merrily on, and our sue- England. cess at Kartoum by force and at Fashoda by firmness, have made a strong impres- sion on Europe. Let us hope that it will be per- manent and salutary. The country has come to be of one mind, and perhaps Lord ROSEBERY has had more to do with this movelty than Lord SALISBURY. The latter was creating a very dis- contented kind of feeling everywhere by his mor- bid desire to give upsomething every time a grave difficulty occurred, and probably the European bservers who have noticed the change since Lord ROSEBERY'S Epsom speech have not been far wrong. There has been a 'decided alteration in our national sentiment, and it could not escape the notice of European Powers. We need not en- ter at any length into an examination of the causes of this change. Perhaps it may be better to take some account of its likely effects. Europe has arranged its own alliances without any regard for English feelings or English interests. We were neglected, and We were not specially interested in the various schemes which were arranged to preserve a peace we had no intention of disturbing. There was a time when Germany would have been delighted to have us as an ally, in her own interests. If we are much more friendly with Germany just now, it is not because we have any intention of joining the league against France, which we have always re- garded as no concern of ours. France seems to have forgotten that the advantages offered us were considerable, and that some strength of purpose was required to resist them. What is still more singular, France has presumed so much on our isolation as to form a policy of making things un- pleasant for us all round, under the belief that we were isolated because we were weak, and that as she could gain nothing towards the Rhine it was her duty to be grasping and querulous everywhere else. Since the accession of Russia to friendship with France this mood has grown. But, on proceeding to improve on former attempts, France .has discovered what Europe as a whole had never ceased to believe—that our isolation was not weakness. France has had to give way, and her patriots are now growling about our "brutal strength." Europe is inclined to be amused at this change of tone, and all that it im- plies. Henceforth we shall be better understood, and there will be loss disposition to treat us as if we were never in earnest in asserting our rights and had lapsed into the heroics of Falstaff. We are now in a position to be valued as a Great Power, and as an:mated by no antagonisms, but as determined to obtain justice and to be rewarded for our efforts. Most likely there will be greater firmness in our diplomatic negotiations, and a st ronger spirit in our advice. Europe extends to us a hearty appreciation. Mocking has passed into praise. It will be our own fault if we slip back again to timiuity and weakness.

Poowe confidence in our police The f lafectionsystem, and in our ordinary methods o Cnme. of moral teaching, ls occasionally shocked by outbreaks of crime which cannot be traced to habitual criminals. There are, however, when we pierce below the surface, two kinds of epidemics in crime, and it is just as well to keep j

them distinct. The criminal classes are keen enough to follow the lead that any daring spirit amongst them chooses to give, and that they act in this way there is abundant evidence tn show. The garotting cases, so common some years ago, were clearly due to the success of this form of attack, and to the pecuniary rewards it yielded. The police were unable to make any very impor- tant captures at first, and the epidemic attained considerable proportions. There have been traces of poisoning cases in this form, and of several other remarkable crimes. Clever brains lead off, and the leas clever follow, until we obtain a suc- cession of almost identical crimes. There may be a suspicion of training in some cases. But, gener- ally speaking, new forms of crime always obt am n a certain amount of success at starting, and then there is a d;sLinct series. It is not an unfair use of the world to call these outbreaks an epide- mic.

The other cases are of a different kind. The attempts to wreck trains made by boys within the last few days, are sufficiently numerous to command attention. They are clearly epidemic in form. The reading of one case urges other boys to do the same thing. Details fix themselves 'on the mind, and there is a disposition to make an experiment. The imitative faculty is always strong in the young, and in cases of this kind it is fair to assume that other faculties must be weak A boy who will seek to wreck a train because he has read an account of how some other boy has tried to do the work is a Hooligan of the worst type. He is weak-minded, and with the weak all epidemics, physical or moral, make considerable havoc. Birching is the best remedy for these mock heroics. Bnt boys of this kind need watching very closely. Grown men, in peculiar assaults on women snd children, have exhibited a tendency to be epidemically affected. Judges have called attention to the fact. After a now notorious publication, describing special offences, there was an outbreak of them in many districts. Sensa- tionalism is then a moral peril. Long newspaper accounts of unhealthy cases are obviously bad. A junlicious pruning is constantly necessary. But we cannot believe that newspapers are wholly to blame, or that our moral teaching is defectiv e The penny dreadful probably has more effect than anything else. The morbid imagination is stimu- lated by stories of crime and adventure. The erratic becomes temporary criminal in consequence. Apparently it is unavoidable. The cure is to punish the guilty parties in such a way as to create an equal effect on the imagination. Deterrents will probably be more effective than anything else. Birching effectively cures mock heroics.

The secret of Germany's commercial develop- meat and success is one which agitates many minds, and innumerable reasons are put forth to explain the fact to the satisfaction of those interes- ted. But as the reasons differ somewhat widely, and there is as much ground for crediting one as another, they are not very convincing or reassur- ing. One of our Consuls has stated that it was simply a matter of discipline, but this is rather an off hand way of solving the question, which is yet unanswered. Other inquirers have attributed Germany's commercial success to her admirable system of technical instruction. We do not, how- ever, think that a specific reason of this character can be reasonably advanced. Our view of the matter is that the descendants of the Fatherland have rapidly awakened to the importance of enterprise, and the many opportunities for pursu- ing it which exist both where commerce has been established, and in places yet unexploited. And once on the right track they have stuck to it and doggedly moved forward. Mr. Consul Powell had added the weight of his opinion to the mass al- ready accumulated on this important subject, and with his views we are inclined to agree. He asserts that the increase of technical and commer- cial shools in Germany is a result, and not one of the causes, of the trade success. It cannot,there- fore, be attributed to technical education. Mr. Powell asserts that it is due to a high state of general education, which contention accords with our opinion. The evident perception of the oppor- tunities comes as a result of this education. All over Germany he says, municipalities are building and equipping commercial schools as an earnest of their intention to keep and develope the trade which has fallen into their hands. As educational matters are proceeding on similar lines in this country there is reason to suppose that we shall not, in the long run, be far behind our German neighbours in the rapid development of our trade with other parts of the world.

Like other arts and sciences that of professional burglary is being continually brought to a higher state of perfection. Likewise, and fortunately for our peace of mind, the skill of our police is main- tained on a par with that of the fraternity which gives them so much trouble. But burglars are not ' only becoming more scientific, they are becoming polite. The burglar of to-day is nothing quite gentlemanly, and moreover possesses a very pretty wit. Our readers will have seen, by the newspaper reports, that the fashion in up-to-date burgling is for the pilferer to leave his card or some other memento of his visit.A letter oftener than not polite awaits the plundered householder on his return from the borderland of sleep, and it is only the apo- logetic or witty character of its contents that pre- vents him from feeling terribly annoyed at the conduct of his unknown guest. This week, the residence of a Sunday evening worshipper in Lon- don was the scene of a burglarious " call." Mr. Owen, the tenant of the premises visited, on his return from Sunday evening service found his goods and chattels much disturbed, many missing, and the following friendly felicities inscribed on a piece of paper covering the clock face : "Sir,— Sorry I could not stop, but we may meet on a future occasion. We have both been praying— you that you might be saved from sin, and me that out of the proceeds of this night's sinning I might save something." Mr. Owen probably hopes that they may meet again, "on some future occasion," but he will prefer the meeting to take place in the Police Court, rather than in his home.

Probably the amateur diplomatiSts in foreign countries will never cease the fascinatinr, task of partitioning the British Empire. It did not mat- ter what views they had, so long as people never listened, but now they have become a power for evil that cannot be ignored, as—in France at any rate—their plans find some approbation. In France there has been formed a small association, or. party, composed of men who enviously look for the partition of the British Empire. The scheme is to promote a better feeling between Franco and Germany, then to see what can be dome by way of working upon the impulsive generosity of the German Emperor in respect of the conquered pro- vinces. They believe that he might one day be induced to proclaim the neutrality of the provinces. The proclamation would endear him for ever to Fretchnaen, who could reduce their army and in- crease their navy. Then an alliance for the des- truction of Great Britain would not present insu- perable difficulties. The war, they believe, would be over in a few months, France taking Egypt, Malta, Singapore, Hong Kong, and Tripoli ; Russia seizing India; Germany, East and South Africa. We are not told who would take England, or what England would be doing daring the partition. It is, however, a striking reminder of the hold this kind of folly has taken upon French imaginations of the baser sort that it should be put forward at the very moment when the policy it favours has sustained a great defeat. If an alliance for the destruction of British power is so easily longed for, why did not Russia support France over Fashoda ? These blundering Anglophobes say that it is no test ; but the attitude of Russia at this crisis is a very pertinent test.

The municipal elections in Warrington have not been extraordinarily interesting, and the results of the five contests contain little in the nature of a surprise for either party. At present the elec- tion is unconcluded, fer the voting in Bewsey Ward has resulted in the two candidates receiving an equal number of votes, and neither being inclined to withdraw, and the Deputy_mayor having declined to give a castirg vote, Messrs. Rogers and Malkin are presumably to have B second tilt at each other. At the present moment a legal problem is agitating the minds of the Cor- poration. There seems to be no precedent for a second contest such as was intended, the fact that Alderman Fairclough declined to give a casting vote making the legality of anoth...r election questionable. Counsel's opinion has been taken but as yet no decision has been received. We are somewhat surprised at Mr. RogerS being able to hold his own, considering the policy of "masterly inactivity" which he has pure sued during his term of office. Bewsey Ward too, had until the rejection of the late Councille- Beaman, been rightly regarded as a Liberal W' . but the opinions of the electors would, at fult glance, appear to have changed. Let us say hr however, that we do not think they have. On .. two occasions that Mr. Rogers has come before the electors there has been a low poll, the reason three years ago being well known. This year the num- ber of electors who have availed themselves of the franchise has increased by 77, of whom only 2'2 have declared in favour of the retiring member,and the remaining M have voted for Mr. Malkin. The figures are not large certainly, but we are n.clined to take them as a good augury. If Mr. Rogers can only poll 22 more votes after throe years' service, then his chances of success are none of the rosiest, especially when his opponent, with the disadvantage of being a new candidate, can obtain an increase of 55 on the figures of his unfortunate predecessor. There were still over 100 electors who abstained from voting and we think it highly probaille that the greater number of these ratepayers would favour Mr. Malkin if they voted at all. Everything tends to prove that Mr. Rsgers polled his full strength and there is every reason to expect that Mr. Malkin's second venture will be attended with success.

The Conservative and liquor party has manage to win a seat in St. John's Ward, where Mr. Nv • Furness failed to repeat his success of three years ago. Councillor Baird was a formidable opponent, and had influence behind him it was impossible for Mr. Furness to withstand. Well! the largest bod 9 of voters in the town has seen fit to return anothei representative of "the trade" to the Ceuncl.ll and we have got to make the best of it. The town has long been dominated by the beer barrel, and we suppose it will continue to until the electors attain to a sufficiently high 0' tellectual standard to comprehend the harmful" ness of it. Either the resources of the War ton Conservative Association are at a ,"

low ebb, or it has openly thrown in its lot with brewing interest. We come to this nib_ conclusion from the fact that the Sankey-, executive appears totally unable to place can' didates in the field who are in a position to take a firm and unbiassed stand on questione touching licensing matters. At present i looks as if a would-be Councillor has onlY to obtain a license, profess Conservatism, and be is assured the support and influence of the Toil organisation.

The results of the municipal elections all over the country show a tufting gain of seats by the Conservatives. There seem to be fifty-nine Coir servative and Liberal Unionist gains, as against thirty-nine for the Liberals. Bolton is, owing to a large addition to the number of its councillor responsible for nearly half the Conservative ur crease. The municipal elections, however, have little party significance. In a large proportion of the boroughs voters are influenced more by nu' portant local questions,than by the mere fact of the candidates being of some particular colour. Of course, in some towns—Warrington for instance —the contests are fought mainly on party lines, but this is by no means the case every though the results must naturally influence relative standing of the political parties on Council. In Widnes, politics were almost h - sight of, the question of the hour relating to the proposed consecration of a section of the cemeterY Thus it is up and down the land, and though so many political gains and losses are spoken of,.tbl do not necessarily follow a contest on politic Issues, or even indicate the way the wind blocs,: The gain of ten labour seats, six of them in Woo Ham, is the only fact of any importance that last week's figures bring out.

The fortnightly meeting of the Council was held at Dutton Wotkoouse on Tuesday. Present :—Mr. J Knowles (chairman), Admiral Jones-Parry, Messrs. T. Lewis, P. Leather, J. Spruce, J. Bllshaw, G. Pilling, T. Wright, P. Gleave, T. Baxtn., J. G. Kif:d, J. M. Wil- liams, W. Bradf ird, W. Turner,J. Stok,s,C. E. Linaker, W. Antwiss, J. Weir, S. Woodwari. H. Talbot, J. W. Baguley, J. Mclntyre, J. B. Cnad wick, J. Ashten (clerk) G. Ashton (deputy clerk), Dr. Adams (medical offic.r), Messrs. Diggle and Swinton (surveyors), and J. Farrini- ton (sanitary inspector). lIRLSBY AFFAIRS. . . - . .

At a meeting of tiire delsby Parochial Cerninittee held on the 31st October, Mr. White presiding, the Clerk real a letter tram Mr. T. C. H. B. Mason intimating that the companies would apply be the court immediately after the vacation to enforce the injunction unless effectual means were taken to divert the se wage fr em the com- panies' property. Another letter dated 13th October from Mr. M aeon stated that six months had now elapsed' since the decision of the Court of Appeal, and during the whole of that time sewage had been constantly passing into the companies' ditches and pipes contrary to the injunction. While, therefore, his clients were willing to give the Ceuncil the tullest opportunity of making per- manent provision for the sewage they could net allow the continuance for an indefinite time of the state of things against which the injunction was directed. 0 her letters veer e read on the same subject dated 18th and 21st October. In the last letter Mr. C. J. Andrews, as- sistant solicitor, stated that the engineer to the Joint Companies was clearly of opinion that the present state of things could not be allowed to continue for the very uncertain period which must elapse before the construction of any works requiring the sanc- tion of the Lecal Government Board, and as no suggestion for meeting this difficulty was made by the eouncil he had no alternative bat to bring the mat- ter before tee court. The Dere also read a letter fr Mr. Radford, and it was resolved that Mr. Radford's lump sum quotation of £lOO as per his letter of the 17th June be accepted, and that he be informed that the rail- way companies were very pressing for the completion of the works so far as they effected them and th a he be requested to put himself into communication with Mr. Johnson at once with a view to ascertaining the wishes of the RailwaV C mepeny. It Was also resolveditat the clerk write te Mr. Meson infer -nine him of the instruc- tions given to Mr. Redford. The minutes were adopted. THE SURVEYOR'S SALARY. The fellowine letter was read :—" Sir,—l am direetei by the Local Gevernment Board to advert to your letter of the 28 butt., with reference to the proposed payment of a commission by the Rural District Council of Run- corn to their Surveyor for the Frodshain district, as an extra fee over that and above his eatery in consideration of the additional work done by that officer in connection with the execution of works ref sewerage and private erode improvement lathe township of Weston. lam to state that, having regard to the provisions of section 193 of the Public Health Act, 1875, the Board question whether the proposed payment which appears to repre- sent percentage up en the amounts of certain contracts is one which could properly be made, lam further to point out that any commission received by the District Council from fr integers in respect of surveyors, superin- tendence and notices in connection with proceedings taken under,' the Privet Streets Works Act, 1892, must be carried to the crebt of the district fund in accordance with the provisions of section 9 (2) of that Act.—l am, sir, vent obedient servant, 11. C. LEWIS, Assistant Secre- tary Local Government Board. The matter was deferred. THE CONDITION OF A FOOTPATH. The following communication was received from the Cheshire County Council :—" Main Roads I am in receipt of your letter of yesterday's (October Roads, as to the condition of the footpath by the side of the main real leading from Sutton Weaver Station to the Old Vicarage Corner in the Parish of Sutten,which I will lay before the main roads and Bridges Committee of this Council at its next meeting.—l am, yours truly, Reginald Potts, Clerk of the County Council." A DANGEROUS BRIDGE AT TECELWALL. A letter was read from Mr. W. Mallard, Clerk to the Urban District Bouncil of Lymtn, calling attention ti the somewhat dangerous condition of the bridge cross- ing the Thelwall Brook, on the road leading into Stathain,and which divides the district of Lymm from Thelwall. It being a boundary bridge the Council pre- sumed that the expeese of repairing the Same would de- volve upon the joint authorities ia which matter they would be glad to hear from the Council. Mr. Swint en (surveyor) said he knew the bridge the Council had under consideration. There was a length of about 10 or 12 yards of District road there. On the suggestion of the Chairman it was unani- lumesly decided that Mr. Swinton inspect the bridge and report to the next meeting. ALLEGED CONTAMINATED RUNCORN WATER. The medical officer reported a case of scarlet fever at Weston Point. It had been alleged that the drinking water from the Runcorn mains became yellow and con- tained grubs. Two mild cases of diptheria were reported from Halton and there were two cases reported at Newton Froilsham. All the case had been visited and the customary orders issued. Var. F arrington sate-1 that the water was not from the Runcorn mains but from an old pump in the vicinity of the place. It would be seen to. The report was passed. COWS AS & MEDIUM FOR INFECTION. Mr. Algernon Fletcher, clerk to the Northwieh Rural District Council, wrote eeelereing the following resolu- tion passed by them at a meeting held on the 28th ult : "That this Council is in favour of cattle being inspected by a duly certified and qualified Veterinary Surgeon, and that the services of such official be paid for out of the Imperial Exchequer, and that before the inspection of any cattle the owner have at least 48 hours notice, aed should any cattle be con- demned by such Inspector the owner to be compensated In full."—" And that a copy of this resolution be sent to all the Councile in Cheshire." Mr. Wright said it was a very important resolution, and be thought they ought to adopt it. In his own township (Halton),a child died from tuberculosis, which the doctor was of opinion had been contracted from a diseased cow. He proposed that the resolution be adopted. Mr. Clarke seconded. Mr. Baxter asked who was going to pay for the cattle. If they were not to know that he should propose that they took n notice of the resolution. From what source was the compensation to be derived. Mr. Woodward sdi the payment to the veterinary surgeon or inspector was by no means the largest sum that would have to he provided. Mr. Talbot thought that it was a question which was above them, and he moved that the letter lie on the table. Mr. Stokes moved a second amendment that the mat- ter be adjourned in order that they might obtain more information. There could not be the least doubt that it was a very important matter. He had himself perhaps suffered more from tuberculosis in cattle than any one present and he knew when the disease got established in stock it was a very serious matter for the farmer. They were the representatives of the public, and they did net come thereto represent their own interests alone. It was a very serious matter when milk was given to , children which came from cows suffering from tubercu- losis. He, therefore thought they ought not to decide the matter without Obtaining further information. Mr. Wood ward believed this question would have to be dealt with.and the acquisition of all the informatien they could poseiblv get was really a step in the right direction. Ele suggested that Mr. Stokes should modify his amend- ment to read that the question be referred to the Par- liamentary Committee. Mr. Stokes accepted the suggestion. Mr. Wright and Mr. Talbot withdrew their motions, and the matter was referred to the Committee.

div.head: VICTIMISING} RUNJORA TRADESMEN.
div.p: VICTIMISING} RUNJORA TRADESMEN.

A number of Runcorn tradesmen have just been vic- timised in no half-hearted fashion. About a fortnight ago a fashionably dressed and prepossessing young lady made her appearance in town and took apartments at a house in Alexandra•terrace, Greenway-road. She gave her name as" Miss Haziehtnst,"and altogether conducted herself as a lady of means. She explained her presence in Runcorn by the statement that her father was an in- valid under the care of a Warrington doctor, who had recommended the atmosphere of Runcorn as likely to suit him, and she had come in advance to make the necessary arrangements. She engaged a house in Green- way-road from Mr. Walter Yarwood, and at her order Mr. J. Fleyes, painter and decorator, thoroughly reties, vated and beautified the interior. In the meantime "Miss flazlehurst "had sever al tons of coal put in the cellar by Mrs. Kniveton,and she ordered from Messrs. T. Leach and Son velvet pile carpets,high-class linoleums,lace cur- tains Sze. Then she became diesatisfied with the house she had chosen, and without giving Mr. Yarwood notice she took a house rented at £4.0 a year in Stanley-villas from Mr. Henry White. Here the lady's taste again proved fastidious, and Mr. Heyes ani a number of men were on Friday set to work painting a4d papering rooms and making certain alterations, but they came to a sudden stop on Saturday, when it was discoyered that " Miss Hazlehurst "had disappeared. During the eight or ten days she had been in town the lady had lived without stint, and Mr. G. Partington, grocer and provision dealer, laments an account of about £6, while Mr. W. riughes, wine and spirit merchant, has supplied nearly 303 worth of bottled beer and stout and brandy, for which he has no equivalent. The lady also" went in" 'for literature. The Misses Mack, besides supp'ying daily newspapers, providad .‘ Miss Hazlehurst " with a num- ber of high-priced periodicals. Fortunately Mr. Leach had not executed his order when his customer so sud- denly took her departure, and Mrs. Kniveton will doubt- less be able to recover her coal.Mr.Heyes is perhaps the greatest sufferer, and on Monday a warrant was taken out for his lavish customer's apprehension. Inquiries have shown that the invalid father was a figment of the imagination. The police have the matter in hand. We believe this "lady "is the one who, about a month ago, similarly victimised a number of Warrington tradesmen, but without transgressing the law.

div.head: EX.ANIINER FRIDAY, NOVEMBER 11, Iq9B
div.p: THE EX.ANIINER FRIDAY, NOVEMBER 11, Iq9B
DEATH OF MR. EDWARD GANDY OF RUNCORN.

The death of Mr. Edward Gandy, which said event took place on Sunday at the Royal Infirmary, Liverpool waith ,r the deceased gentleman had goae t untiego an operation, removes from our midst a man whose innate geniality and broad Cons:lan sympathies won him the respeci of a large circle of triends,to whom his untimely end has come as an acute shock. Mr. Crandy's connee. tioa with Runcora and with the public life of the town, wtaieti always commanded his best energies, has been a long and nonaurable one. He was one of those men— and they are rare—whose iaterest and personal ven3ra• 'tion for their native town suffer no change by th 3 vary- ing mutations of progress or denay.Runcorn WAS to him in his later years what it was to him as a boy—a place whirr, in all that was best in a man might be expended for the good of his fellows and in furtherance of the many social and religious agencies which go to make up the life of a community.Na man had a deeper love for all Work which had as its fundamental basis the moral and spiritual updfting of his fellows than dr. Gandy, and no man did mire, either by s..eliaabnegaion or caoscientious duty to practice waat tie taiight. Gifted by nature mull a genial personality which fascinated by the sheer force of its magnetic influence, Mr. Gandy was peculiarly fitted to exercise a potent power over young and impressionable minds. As a private citiz en, or an alert business man ; as a local preacher or a Sunday school teacher, he was ever trie same, courteous and full of Sunny optimism which reflected tce taits by which tie himself was always dominated and sustained. Though a Free Methodist, and one of the origin al founders of Ellesmere-street Free Methodist Church, of which place of worship he reinsjn3,l the chief support up to his death, Mr. Gandy was never an extremist in religious matt:a.s. Be withheld his approval from no morment, whatever its designation,whica embraced as its cardinal doctrine the gospel of Jesus Christ ; and it Says MUcts for a man's character that amid the storm ' and s;ress of occasiona, religious diff3rences in the town Mr. Gandy never once forfeited the respect of friend or foe. He was a man of many parts, all of which ne played successtully. As a preach ir he was sound and persuasive, and in public debate he was regarded as o 3s- Nash:lg exceptional amity. On Tuesday the usual firtniehtly meeting of the above Board was held at the D atton Workhouse, there being present : Messrs. J. Mosley Williams (chairman). A. It. Norman, J.P., J. Meadowcroft, T. Reynolds, and the Rural District Councillors, with Mr. J. Ashton (clerk), and Mr. George Ashton (deputy clerk). THE GUARDIANS AND THE NURSING STAFF, miss T. G. Lowndes, secret try te the Northern Work- house Nursing Association, wrote under date Oetober 26h asking if the Board accepted Norse Todd at the salary named in her jotter of the 29th September viz £2B and £2 for uniform. Nurse Todd had had maternity training and held certificates for the same,betides which she had had 1 years experience at Gateshead. Hie re- commended Norse Todl as being the most experienced nurse at liberty. 'raiser experienced nurses did not go for a salary of £25. If, therefore, the beard only wished to give this salary would they be good enolgh to retain Nurse Todd till she could send the other nurse recom- mended in her letter of October 18th, Nurse Lowe,aged 30, trained at Birmingham, who would be ready at the end of December. Miss Lowndes wrote again under date October 29th, stating that she was desired by her committee to say that if the nurses were in future appointed for two years the time off duty for the day nurse must be increased, as the committee were of opinion that once a week was not sufficient re- laxation or opportunity of going out for a nurse, if she was to keep her health and carry on her duties satisfac- torily. The majority of Union Infirmaries allowed their nurses now off duty time either every day or every other day. They were aware that the nurse asked for more time off duty and was refused. As regarded any eorre 3• pondenee between the nurses and herself (Miss Lowndes) the committee considered that a nurse was perfectly justified in wishing promotion and higher salary and in accepting such when available, and as the Board refused to raise Nurse Willis' salary to £3O when Nero Barris left she considered it molest; to apply for an increase again. The committee would still reserve to themselves the right to withdraw a nurse if the conditions of her life were not comfortable or happy. As Norse Tod l's time with the Association expired in fifteen months the committee thoueht it advisable that she should remain temporarily at Dutton as iffered till the other nurse was ready in Dscember who could ;Ito for two years at a salary of £2s,rising £1 yearly and uniform exceeding to their terms. The Chairman : Ibis scarcely to our satisfaction.

IVIL 4. R. Norman thought th;.ot as tar as the nurses were concerned the only question that was raised was that of "off time." In that letter the Council were accused of refusing the nurses both in that matter and in respect of their salary. He ',wished to roint out that it was not so, and those questions had not been before them at all. When the arrangements were made the last time the nurses were befor3 them, they expressed their entire satiefaction at the offer of the Board. On Monday evening 'a further step towards making a c west inevitable was taken when the Church patty met at the Pariih Church Schools and selected four can- did ites tor their representatioa on the Runcora School Hoard. The gentlemen selected were the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, and Messrs. E. Liaison, Joseph Prit- chard and John Littler. The result of this selection will be that, if the candi- dates are elected, the Voluntary School Party will hold the balance of power in their hands, because there is little or no doubt enter-aintect but the Rev. Father Gore will be elected—in fact nothing can stop hint getting on the Board—therefore, it is perfectly clear that seine st iady and consistent woik must be done on the part of the undenominati inal party it they wish to have a trifle inure to say in the gov3rnment of matters educa- tional. At the outset it was thought that a compromise would be made and that the undenomivational representatives would be five,the Church three, and the Roman Catholic one, but as the Church party fail to see justice in this, and the undenominational section(who have the greatest lain) fail to see justice in the alternative, it is now generally expected that five candidate; will be run by the latter body, and a hold bid made for the balancing seat. div.head: SXILOR'S SAD END.
div.p: A SXILOR'S SAD END.
THE RUNCORN " DEA:TEI TRAP."

On Turieday at Runcorn Police COW.; Mr.J. E.Worsley, coroner, hell an inquest on the body of Anton Yanson, aged 18, fireman on board the steamer Schwaigaard of Bergen, who was found drowned in the Weston Canal on Monday morning. Mr. Nilssoreho acte I as interpre- ter and was duly sworn in that c apacity. 0 'car Larson, fireman on the Schwaigaard, through the interprete-, deposed that h.s home was at Christian- sued. His ship was lying at the lay-by on the Snip Canal. On Sunday evening about seven o'clock the do- oeaei and himself left the ship and were in Runcorn for attar half an hour or threequarters. They returned along the dock side; he did not know the way they went exactly. There we-e lights but they were far from them. There was china clay on the quay side bat it was not y.-ry slippery. It was a dark night. Witness walk:d about six yards in advance of the deceased, and when they were approaching the bridge(at Purr's Lock) witness shouted to the deceased to look out for the dock. At that momont dace ase I slipped on one toot an I went head first into the water. He did not sink at once and witness lay fiat on the quay side and tried to reach the deceased but be could not do so. He then looked around and found a spade, but he failed to reach the deceased with thisond in) ran to a schooner and shouted for help bit there did not appear to be anybody on board, as no person came. When he gotbsck the deceased had disappeared. Witness could swim but not enough to keep a person up, He did not know whether the deceased could swim or not, They were bort' sober ; they had not touched anything while they were in Runcorn. Witness did not think it was the Cuba clay which caused the deceased to slip. H' thought he was too near the edge of the quay. Mr. W. Jones (a juryman) inquired if a handrail could not be placed at that part of the canal. M.. W. Slaw (Seamen's Missionary) sali there was a nil there. Mr. Jones replied that it was very low and a, person coull c itch the rail and " pop over.'' Another Juryman said a new road wanted making over the place. Dv. W. Suaw depopad to recovering the hely on Mon- day morning from Parr's Lock P.O. Upton said he was pres.ent when the body was 'wavered. He had it taken to the mortuary and there he examined it. There were no marks of violence and no money in the pockets of the clothing. The place where the accident occurred was slippary with 'Mina clay: The C nailer said it seemed to have been a pure acci- dent. It was very sad that such a promising young man should be lost in this way. A verdict of " Accid drowned" was returned.

div.p: cA.PITA I. GHAT.

I have heard some particulars connected with the gale of Mr. Harry erCilmont's steam yacht Giralda to the Spanish Government at the beginning of the war which go to show that the authorities at Mad• rid were at that time quite as apprehensive of a revolution at house as of defeat abroad. As a matter of fact, the Queen Regent's advisers were so convinced that the populace would get beyond con- trol that their plans for Her Niajesty's flight with the King to Austria were all cut and dried, and the Giralda was the craft in which the voyage to Trieste was to have been performed if emergency arose. Drawings of the vessel were submitted to the Queen R ,gent, and it was not until her approval had been signified that the bargain with Hr. licCalmont was Cruck. The Technical E lueation Board of London has had presented to it a very valuable educational col- lection of over 21,000 natural history specimens. as well as a quantity of literatuee classified to corres- pond wilh the collection. The specimens will be accommodated temporarily in the great hell of Aske's School, Hoxton. To be of real value they need to be associated with a classroom and a bio- logical laboratory. It is intended to give special privileges to teachers with their pupils to visit the collectioa, and to arrange that a portion of the collection may be available for loan to schools and other institutions where natural history specimens are desirable. The remarks of the Lord Chief Justice the other day in reference to the sale of liquor at the bars in Ithe Houses of Parliament will compel the Govern- ' ment, for mere decency's sake to introduce a Bill at the be,sinning of next session for the purpose of putting the traffic on a legitimate footing. Although the legal Proleedingß applied only to one of the bars, at which drink was supplied to strangers having business either at the C Immittees or the lobby, or visiting either House out of curiosity, the Lord Chief Justice's criticism applied also to the bars at, which refreshments are sunplied to mem- bers. It is quite possible that the Kitchen Commit- tee may abolish the sale of liquor at all the bars ot the House next session till a short amending Bill is passed. The temperance party, who have scored a triumph, will opnose the Bill in every way, and the Government will have to force it through, for the convenience of members by the use of the closer Profound regret is everywhere expressed at the death of Mr. T. B. Potter, who for an unbroken period of exactly thirty years represented Richard Cobden's former constituency in Parliament, and during that time never failed to uphold the princi- ples of his great predecessor. Mr. Potter was per- haps the most sturdy exponent of the Manchester School of Liberalism of whom the present genera- tion has had knowledge. The founder and moving spirit of the Cobden Club, he devoted his energies, his time, and his money to the propagation of Cob- denism. With all his fighing qualities, he was the most lovable of men, and his popularity at Roch- dale was equalled by the esteem and affection in which be was held by men of all parties in the House of Commons. It was a keen disappointment to Mr. Potter when on his withdrawal from Parlia- mentary life in 1895 his old constituents elected a Conservative to succeed him—the first Tory mom. bar who had sat for Rochdale for nearly forty years. I believe that some years earlier he had felt even more acutely the political estrangement which arose between himself and Mr. John Bright over the Home Rule question. Mr. Bright did nothing to soften the poignancy of the situation. Hie eldest son was chosen to oppose the veteran Free Trader. Mr. Potter won, as he had always won, but the episode left a painful impression. Among other in- cidental results, it evoked a letter from Mr. Glad- stone, in which in glowing terms that statesman expressed his admiration lot the life and work of his devoted follower. The dealers in milk in London are about to be exposed to the competition, upon an extensive scale, of the French producer of mills. A powerful syndi- cate has been formed here for the purpose of importing it. I do not understand that it is a French enterprise. The stab to the English dairy farmer comes from nearer home. Even a member of the council of the Dairy Farmers' Association has become one of the syndicate. The farmer may not suffer immediately, as he is probably protected by contracts which have a certain time to run, or require a certain notice; but to a large extent he must look upon his business as seriously menaced. The adulteration laws will operate against the syndicate and the retail dairyman quite as effectu- ally at they do in the case of English milk: hut the consumers will have no protection in the matter of the cleanliness of the foreign dairies or the health of the foreign animals.

div.head: REV Y, YONOE ON _"7IIE LORD'S
div.p: REV Y, YONOE ON _"7IIE LORD'S
SUPPER."

Preaching on this subject in Wycliffe Church last Sunday eveaine, Mr. Yonge said tnat he believed the ordinance of the Lord's Sipper to be a veritable, valu- able, and valid ni cans of grace to sincere and spiritual rec'plents, wherever it is believingly observed, in what- ever form and manner ; wte t ler administ-red from so-called alters, by so-called priestly hand, amid ornate ritual and in gorgeous cathedrals, or in the lowliest con- venticles, amid humb'est and plain-st surroundings, by preachers and people of least attainment either of education or refinement. " Wherever two or three are gathered together in My Name, there am I in the midst of them." Any such "two or three,"if they truly desire to keep the feast in remembrance of their Lord, are entitled to do so, and will be blessed and benefitted in deing so. This is the New Testament idea. This was the practice of the earliest believers. Therefore it is our assured faith that we here, at this table, di observe the Lord's supper eccording to the Lord's will, and with experience of the L eel's blessing. Whatever be the"g,race"conveyed to the believer in and by this Ordinance, it is so co 1- veyee here, as truly as it can be conveyed any- where else. It is necessary to assert this, because many persons busily dispute and flatly deny it. It is being decayed by upholders of this sacredotal idea and the priestly clase, that this Ordinance as observed here is nothing but a spurious, fal,e and mischievous pretence. It is said that Non-Episcopal Churches are not true churehes of Christ, and that mieisters who have not recrived Episcopal ordination are not true ministers. Our churches are unauthorized and our minis- try is unauthorized, and c onsequently our sacraments are unautnorized and can only had astray. But which are we to believe? The testimony of our own spiritist consciousness, which tells us that here, at this Table, by meens of this Ordinance, as we observe it, we do have fellewship with Christ, or, are we to believe the asser- tien of the sacerdotalists that our Ordinance is vain ? We prefer the evidence of our own spiritual senses, and maintain that here we know Christ in the braking of the bread, and do " feed upon Him in our hearts by faith and with thanksgiving." We bow our very souls as in His actual presence. We say in the language of the Apostle Peter, " Lord, it is food for us to be here. Let us build Tabernacles.' We would stay upon this Mount of Vision, but going back to life we feel that we " have been with Jesus," that we have been fed with " the bread of God," cheered with the wine of Heaven's love, and inspired with the joys of G od's salvation. Are we to contradict all this, to abandon L, at the word of the humanly instituted priest, who bids us b ^neve that until he consecrates bread and wine upon the alone altar of his church there can be no true Lord's supper at all? The demand is too great, and we derline to make it. We say that whatever reality there is in the Ordinance it is as real here as upon the Attars of St. Elphin's or St. Alban's. Whatever contact with Cerist it affords can be formed as truly here as there. The Lord's presence, whether in or at the Sacrament, depends, not upon any invoking word of an officiating ministereet him be called "priest" or by any other title ; but it depends upon the Lord's own will, and His Will is to be ever present to believing souLs, and by means of these outward and material symbols to give thern tangible assurance and pledge of His Presence, His Power, and His Love. H tying referred to the wave of Protestant feeling that was now passing through the country, Mr. Yonge said he believed the duty of the Free Evangelical Churches was to put themselves in the forefront of this move- ment, and to do all in their power to resist and defeat the attempt at priestly sepremacy. Here, in the matter of the Lord's Supper, was one especial respect in which such resistance cauld be offere I. The Archbishop of Canterbury had been the first Archbishop since the re- formationtoaffirm that the doctrine of con-sub stantiation was permissible in the Church of England : but that the Berrien Doctrine of rransubstantion was not permissible. Only those used token discernment of sub-le distinc- tions could find much el erence between the one and the other. But neither are according to any teeching of the New Testament, and both depend upon the priestly function to bring them to pass. But the true, spiritual experience of Christ's presence at His Table was abso- lutely independent of any priestly interposition. The Lord's Supper is as valid when the hu nblr st layman pre- sides at it, as when the moat regularly appointed minis- ter does so. In some senses, perhaps, the humbler the offlciant the better. It is not the human, but the Divine that is neceesary. It is not man we come te meet. bet Christ, and that is the best Communion service which :nest sends us away with the feeling that" We hive seen the Lord."

div.head: LIVERPOOL DIOCES&N CONFERENCE.
div.p: LIVERPOOL DIOCES&N CONFERENCE.
The seventeenth annual conference of the clergy snd Laity of the Liverpool diocese was opened at St. Gorge' e Hall, Liverpool, on Tuesday morning..
PROPOSED CHURCH ROUSE.
At the afterno)n sitting. the Conference passed a resolution in commendation of the Church House scheme, towards which £17,537 has been subscribed.
THE RIGHTS AND DUTIES OF THE LAITY._

The su;ieco for discussion, " The Rignts and Duties of the Laity," was introduced by Mr. Charles M'Arthur, M.P., Lord Balcarres, M.P. The debate was considerably enlivened by the Rev. John Wakeford, who denied that the House of Commons was the governing body of the Church. He referred to the surroundinga of that chamber as" the thick atmos- phere of inspissated ignorance," but at the request of the Bishop he withdrew the phrase. el Mr. WeAbtook (Warrington) said that no Church was so rich in able and int Tec-ual laymen as the Church of !Ragland, but for some reason they were not enrolled in the work of the Church as they should be. There was a vast body of laity standing idle lithe market-place. One reason for this was that the laity themaelves did not realise that they had any rights, while the clergy did not acquaint them as often as they ought to do. Lay helpers complained thLt they were not cordially treated by the clergy, and if a bridge of sympathy could be erec- ted between clergy and laity, there would be less room fest suspicion of patronage and conceit on the part of the clergy. No doubt the laity had their weakness. and the eleargy had theirs, (Laughtes.) It was the duty of the laity to read the Bible, study the Prayer Book, attend church, bear up nobly against dry sermons—(laughter) —and c-,ntribute towards the support of the Church and ministry. How many of them spent more on tobacco than on their religion ? (Hear, hear.) It was the duty of the laity also not to be brawler. Of all sports, parsonbaitinz was the worst,and he had heard it likened to shooting tame birds. (Laughter and applause.) The Rev. E. C. E. Carletoa (Warrington) said that the laity were largely to blame for the difficulties and dis- order that arose in the Church. For 130 years they had left the Church without a governing body, and it was not suerising that there should be lawlessness. He ad- vised a return to the primitive principles by which Churchmen were allowed a voice in the selection of bishops. In the evening, "The Increased Secularization of Sun- day" was under consideratien WEDNESDAY.

STRONG REMARKS..I3-iTiE-li-EV. A. M. MITCHELL, The Liverpool Diocesan Conference was continued on Wednesday. Mr. W. S. Barrett real a paper upon the work of the Church ii colliery and chunical districts, and urged the need of increased support far all Church agencies in such rpizhbourhoods. He moved—" That this Con- ference, while thankfully acknowledgine the spiritual wok already done in the colliery and chemical dis- tricts in the dioe,ease, considers that increased support I should be extented to all Church agencies in such dis- tricts " _ .

—.— The Rev. J. Wright Willimns seconded the resolution. He said that he had had eight years' esperience of Widnes, and while there WRS certainly a large amount of sulphuretted hydr)gen in the localitv—(laughter)— there was a still larger amount of noble-hearted and earnest Christian endeavour among the men and women of the district.

_ The Rev.J.G. Hulley (Skelrnersdale) spoke of the en- couraging position of the work among colliers. The Rev: A. M. Mitchell said he had intended to move an amendment to the effect that the Conference should express its active sympathy with those wh3 were engaged in the colliery and chemical districts, as far as ' their physics' and social needs were concerned. He be- lievld the Bishop did not approve ef such an amend- merst, and he regrettA that it should ha en, because physical and social needs—call them secular if they liked —were quite as important as what were called spiritual needs. As to the chemical divr;cts,he a aid that Widnes as eVerrboly knew, was a hell on earth—(" No. no. ") I --and St. Helens was a second hell on earth. ("No. no") Such at least was his opinion, and it was the opinion of a great many more. (" No, no.") They had this fact to face, at any rate, that the collier and those who lived in the chemical district had to live under the most try- ing and the most unsatisfactory conditions. They were engaged in unhealthy employment •, their lives were shortened by the employment in which they were en- gaged, and men, women, boys and girls were sent into an park, grave. He knew this applied in connection with Widnes, They knew such a thing had taken place in connection with the making of matches and in the pottery districts;yet here were men making money out of three people.men who would not comply with the simple conditions of the law, .and see that the ordinary safe-

_ guards were provided,because they were so full of greed because the lust of gain was upon them, and they cared not for the lives of the workers, and their hands were stained with blood. Another fact was this, that people were not merely slowly killed in the chemical and other unhealthy occupations, but they were sometimes sud- denly deprived of life,and the first thought of employers in such cases was," How can we wriggle out of paying compensation 2" Mr. W. S. Barrett : Absurd l This is absolutely in- cc' rect. I The Rev. A. M. Mitchell It cannot be incorrect. I because I know of cases within my own knowledge. Mr. W. S. Barrett : It is incorrect. _ . .
Wit-, Rev AM Mitchell; -"ltiS-Wo-t-wincorrect so far as my information is concerned. It may ta so far as Mr. Barrctt's information is concerned. I would like to ask

this—le the Church of England prepare 1. speaking through the Diocesan Conference to-day, to say to the employers, " There is the Compensation Act, and we mean to stand by the people, and ae3 that that Compen. sation Act is faithfully and righteously administered ?" Proceeding the speaker referred to overcrowding in urne districts and the lack of sanitation. and added that when a clergyman of a parish spoke out and endeavoured to make the medical officer of health and tile sanitary insmectar d 3 toeir duty, such a one was regarded as an extreme Radical, a danger to the Church and to the whole community, and a determined effort was made to suppress bim. Toe R3V. G. R. Garrett remarked that Widnes was not such a pace as the previous speaker would lead them to suppose. (Applause ) The health reports showed that it did not stand very high as regarded the death rate. The chemicals were so s:roag that no germs and no microbes could live. (Laughter.) The Rev. Canon Mitchell of Prescot, said that when one ,g,tt acquainted with colliers it was astonishing what nice fellows they were, even toe roughest of them. He had always found the employers of the distric: most sympathetic and kind to their employees in times of trouble or accident.
Mr. Lyon G Abourne, a collier of twenty-four years' standing, said that colliers likd to hear the pure word of God, which they hardly ever got in any of the churches.

'fee Bishop said that his ow a experience proved that colliery pr ,prietors and chemical proprienrs were by no means the worst of men. (Hear, hear.) He believed the cAliers and chemical workers weri a class of men who were well thought of, and well provides for, and who enjoyed the goodwill of thAr masters. He would not be doing his duty if he did not bear strong testi. mony to what he had seen and what he knew of the masters.
Thq resolution was then a looted. RELIGIOUS EDUCATION.

Regarding the subject of -r-e-iiii-o-u-s—Olucation in the upper and middle c'asses, the Cooterea3e adopted Canon Blundell's resolution as to th, question requirin4 more careful attentim on th 3 part of toe Church than it bad hitherto received,

The Rev. M. &evenson, principal of the Warrington Traming College, said the two great difficulties in the way ot dealing with the problem of religious education were the sense!ess clamour raised of late years against the teaching ot doctrine, and the kind of religious know. ledge tests in conn-ction with the Oxford and Cambridge examioations now in vogue. Re moved the following Tiler, which was also" adopted :—" That a Board of Examiners be appointed in the diocese, empowered to authorizi examinations in religious knowledge in secondary schools under the authority of the Bishop, this Board to be nominatod by the teachers of such schools throughout the dicc:aa with the consent of the Bishop."

Dr. SEPIITON : I have been there and could not smell Toole's beyond the yard • Longford was worse. Mr. KNOWLES : Well. lay. Mr. Dzes said they had ordered the new dryer daring the month of June, and they could not get delivery. The whole scheme had ben mapped oat and carefully gone into by the Committee. As they knew, they had had a long continued dry season. Last year it had been all experimental work. If they had plenty of water there would be no

WARRINGTON V. LANCASHIRE INDEPENDENT COLLAGE.— These teams met at Malley Range on Saturday. War- ringt on won the toss and elected' to play towards the .town goal. A fine movement `-y the Warrington right wing and centre ended in E. Connor scoring the first goal. From the kick off the Collpge rushed down and scored. Up to half time the game weat all in favour of Warrington, E. C nnor obtaining two more goals, both from good individual play. Half time r Warrington, three goals ; College, one goal. On resuming Warriugtoa continued te have 'all the play, obtaining four more goals—R. Roberts three, F. Jewkeo, one. Final SCOW :-- Warrington, seven goals ; Collage one. WARRINGTON S. ELPIIIN'S V. WIZIST)N RAMBLERS.— Played at Warringtoa on Saturday afternoon. Hunter and Taylor were away front' the home side. The Ramblers started against t'ae breeze, and by smart dribbling they were enabled to attack first. Chesworth was especially prominent in maintaining the aggressive. and the Sahel; were compelled to concede a corner, Duckworth cleared, only to see Moss again test Hall, who saved. Walton dribb'el well and the visitors were now forced to defend, Prescott effecting a fine. clearance from a penalty. Con- certed play by the Warringtonians saw Johnion tested, and the subsequent clearance was met by Bradshaw who ishot wildly. Mos; tricked the two Singletons, and the Ramblers got dangerously near, only to find their efforts met by a itubborn defence, The game waged even, and the only dangerous shet for any time was a screw by Moss, which Hall cleared. Adamson placed a free kick well for the visitors, but it was all to no purpose, for Hall could not be defeated. • Eventuelly the Whistom Men were penalized, and Duckworth kicking well to his forwards Hatton scored easily. Prescott almost osme neat-denting for the visitors a moment later; and Hall was applauded for effecting twO fine saves. The game continued in Whiston's favour, and the home team were severely pressed. St. Elphin's now broke away, and Singleton shot, the ball going wide. Whiston were not having all their own way. From a goal kick Hall placed the ball well up the field, but the visitors drove it back. From now to the conclusion of this half Moisten held the upper hand, although they could not score. Half time—St. Elphin's tone, Vihiston Ramblers nil. In the second half St. Elphin's load the best af •matters, and in- crtased their score by three goal', whilst Whisten had to be satisfied with one. Jones, Duckworth, the two Singletons, and 'Hall were the pick of the norne team, while Prescott, Mole, Walton, and Chesworth were the mainstay of the visitors. In the second half Earlestown had matters all their own way, Skelmersdale never once becoming dangerous, and they ran oat victors by 8 goals to 1.

div.head: FARLESTOWN A.ND NEWTON
div.p: FARLESTOWN A.ND NEWTON
AN ACKNOWLEDGEMENT.

The Rev. J. Hirst desires to acknowledge with I thanks the receipt of 25 articles of clothing from the South Lancashire Needlework Guild for the Police Court and Prison Gate Mission of the Liver- pool Diocesan C.E.T.S. P.S.A.

At the usual meeting of this society held on Sunday afternoon, there was a good attendance. Mr. J. Hatton presided, and an interesting address was given by the limy. E. Bocock, who took for his subject "Conscience." Miss E Clarke sang in excellent voice "Eternal rest," and "The lost chord," and Miss Newton recited "Beautiful snow." PLEASANT SATURDAY_ EVENING.

The P.S.A. Society have made a departure from the ordinary course, and gave a pleasant evening on Saturday. There was a good number of people present, and Mr. B. Barker presided. Mr. G. Thing gave a capital address, and recitations were sub- mitted by Mies Coates of Ilaydock, and Mr. Wilson of Earlestown. Mr. G. Clarke gave a Lancashire reading, Mr. Wilson a couple of mouth organ solos, and Mr. Baton a banjo solo. Mr. S. Dring presided It the piano. Si. JOHN'S CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL.
The members of the young men's senior scholars'

class attached to the above S—unday school, inaugur- ated on Saturday evening a series of social even- ings. There were over 100 people present and after partaking of refreshments,dancing was indulged in, Mr. J. Warhurt‘n officiating as M.C, Mr. Peplow's band supplying the music. During an interval Miss M. Walton sang "A Dream of Paradise.' The evening was very pleasantly spent, great credit being due to the committee for the excellence of the arrangements. SUDDEN DEATH AT EARLESTOWN. On Saturday evening an old man named Thomas Woodward about 63 years of age, of 15, Clarence street, Earlestown, died rather suddenly. In the afternoon the people with whom he lodged were erecting a hen coop, and he was superintending it. All at once be said "Take me in." He became unconscious, and was carried into the house and Dr. Watkins sent for, but there was no hope and the man died in the evening. He was injured at the Wood pit explosion in 1878, and has since been In the receipt of a pension. SlisstoNAar MEETING AT IVARGILA.VE The usual annual meeting in connection with the

Society for the Propagation' of the Gospel in Foreign parts was held in the Wargrava Schoolroom on Wednesday evening. The Rev. J. Carson presided, but there was only a moderate attendance. The Rev. A. Homer from South Australia attended as a deputation, and delivered an interesting address on the work of the Society in the Antipodes, his remarks being illustrated by limelight views, the lantern being under the charge 61f Mr. Lawson. A collection was made in aid of the funds. POLICE CASES. At the Earlestown Police Station on Friday morning before Mr. J. W. Emmett, Katherine Law- less of no fixed abode, was charged with vagrancy in King-street, and was sent to gaol for 14 days.— At Newton on Saturday morning before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, Daniel Brown was charged with being drunk and was fined 23. 61. and costs.—At Earles- town on Monday before. Mr. C. B. F. Borron, Daniel O'Donnell for being drunk, and George Mather for sleeping out, were each fined 2s 6d. and costs. PRIMITIVE METHODIST HOME MISSIONS. In connection with the above special services Were held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel,Earle,- town, on Sunday. The preacher at the morning service was announced as the Rev. G. H. Birch, but I as he was unable to be pre ient owing to indisposi- tion a student officiated in his stead. In the even- ing an interesting sermon was preached by the Rev. E. Bocock. On Wednesday evening the usual an- nual meeting in connection with the same object was held in the chapel. Mr. T. Beaman presided,l in addresses on Hems Mission work were given by the Revs. G. H. Birch, and E. Bocock. NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL LITERARY SOCIETY. The usual weekly meeting of this Society was held on Monday evening under the presidency of the Rev. James Allatt There was a goad attend- ance of members. The night was devoted to impromptu speeches in which most of the members took part. Amongst the subjects debated were— " Anarchy " ; " Why do blacksmiths use sand" ; "Gas workers (stokers) working 78 hours ; is it too long ?" It was contended by various speakers that the Newton Urban District Council ought to set an example to other labour employers by reducing the hours that these m-n work. " Ought horse racing to be stopped," &c., &c. The Society has now about 40 members enrolled, and at the next meeting a reading will be given by varioas members on Shakespeare's" Merchant ot Venice." GOOD TEMPLARY.

The quarterly meeting of the Hope of Earlestown lodge of Good Templars was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall, on Monday evening. Bro. T. Cutler pre- sided end there was a large attendance of members. Three candidates were admitted to membership,and several others were proposed. Letters were read from the Gleam of Sunshine lodge, Tranmere,relat- ing to a visit in January next, and from the Wesley Hall Lodge, Liverpool, re a visit in December. The Secretary's quarterly report was of an encouraging nature showing active work had been carried on, and that there was an increase in membership. The Financial Secretary,and Treasurer's reports showed S good balance in hand. The election of officers resulted in the following being elected: Bro. T. Culter, C T ; Sister Woods, V T; Bro Barker, secre- tary; Bro Parker. F secretary; Bro J Warburton, treasurer; BroJ Woods, chaplain; Bro J Singleton, marshall ; Sistel Preston, assistant secretary ; Sister Smith, D ; Bro Pope, G Bro Waring, sen- tinel; Bro J Hatton installing officer. SOUTH LANCABHIRR BRANCH OF Tan NRRDLE- WORK GUILD. The annual exhibition of garments and clothing made by the vice-presideats and associates of the Needlework Guild took place in the Town Hall, Newton, on Friday afternoon. There was a moder- ate attendance including Mrs. Royse (president), Dr. J. W. Watkins, Mrs. F. E. Miller, Miss Watkins (hon. sec.), Misses Brierley, &c. Mrs. Rom de- livered her annual address, which was very en- couraging. This year there were 58 groups and about 2,000 associates who had sent in 2.808 arti- cles. Clothing had been sent to the Armenian re- ' fugees from the Earlestown Committee and other institutions covered by the Guild operations in- cluding Warrington, Wigan, Ashton, Flavdoek, Newton, Burtonwood, Collins Green, Winwick, &c. The committee desired Mrs. Rorie to remain their president although she has removed to Kent. Mrs. Royse consented, and will assist the Guild as much as possible.

div.head: ST,. HELENS.
div.p: ST,. HELENS.
A s'r. HELENS RASCAL PUNISHED.

EgThomaB Glynn, of Glover-street, a St. Helens youth who has a very unenviable record, was on Saturday sent to prison for siK weeks' hard labour on a charge nf assaulting Constable John Hall. The constable said that, along with Constable Platt, h. was in plain clothes shadowing some people in Tontine-street, when prisoner and a companion interfered with thern,and Glynn ran at him and kicked him.
ACCIDINT AT A PARR COLLTERY.

George Br-o;n-l-n-w-,- Vge-d-srx-t-een—y—e-s-r;,-Who resiled with hisiparents at 313, Cliosley-lane, Raydock, has been admitted to the Haydodc Cottage Hospital with both aims badly broken. Brownlow was employed at the Sothport pit of Measrs R. Evans and Co., situated at Parr,St. Helens, and was unhooking a rope off a waggon at the pit when the cage started up the shaft, and be- fore Brownlow could get clear his arms were jammed against the woodwork and smashed.
APPOINTMENT OF A ST. HELENS CONGREGATIONAL ItImsTER. . .

During the morning service at the St. Helens Congrr- gational Chhch on Sunday, Mr. J. J. Dutton, secretary of the church, read a letter frpcn the Rev. F. W. Clarke, 8.A., of Frome, Semerset,in reply to a request, made at a specially called church meeting last Wednesday night asking the rev. gentleman to accept the position as pastor of the church in succession t 9 the Rev. J. A. Mitchell, B.A. In the communication Mr. Clarke said be had decided to accept the call of the church,

rI At St. Helens Police Court en Monday a case was heard in which Margaret Fluy.on, 18 VPATS of age, of Wbeatfield-street,claimed an order upon Poll nflatable ce- Henry Wilkes, of the borough police forc, in respect to the sunpert of her child. me. E. W. Swift appeared on her behalf, and Mr. FL L. The complainant dersed that on one occasion the defendant! got her into the police barracka,where he lived,and that she stared there until four o'clock in the morning. The defence was a denial of the qirl's story as to the defend- ant's intimacy with her, and it was contended there was not sufficient evidence of corroboration. After a hearing of some hours the bench intimated that they would not tflake any order in the ease,

div.head: EWTON URB A.N DISTRICT COU CIL.
div.p: EWTON URB A.N DISTRICT COU CIL.

This Council met at the Town Hall, Earl.st-iwn. on Monday afternoon, Mr. C. B. F. Boron, JP., C.C., pre- sided, and there were also pr,snit :—Dr. Patters in, Messrs. W. Coiling wood, J. W. Emmett, J.P., P. Mc- Mahon, J. Simpson, W. Thompson, W. Beatty, J. ES. Forster, E. T. Evans, T. Ormand, with Mr. W. W. Shirley (clerk), Mr. R. Brierley (survayor)- and Mr. A. Bowes (assistant surveyor).

div.head: OTES OF CONDOLENCE.
div.p: OTES OF CONDOLENCE.

The Chairman said before the business commenced he should like to refer briefly to the loss the district had gust tined by the cl-ath of the Rev. Mr. Monk. He had occupied the position of vicar for upwards of 30 years. and been brought prominently before the public. He was sure the members of the Council were grieved at the loss sustained by his removal, and they must sympathise with his relations in their log. He (the Chairman) ha I also to refer to the affliction which had occurred to Mr. Gilmour by the loss of his wife. The members of the Council, he was sure, sympathised with Mr. Gilmour in the loss he had sustained.—The Chairman then moved that votes of condolences be sent to the relatives of the Rev. H. Moak aad Mr. Gilmour. Mr. Evans seconded, and the resolution was unani- mously carried. THE ABSENCE OF MR. STONE.
The Chairman said he had to apologise for the absence of Mr. Stone wno was detained in London. GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.

This committee recommended that the Clerk write to Mr.J.Littler, of Market-street,Earlestown,calling his at- tention to the waste of water at his premises and the loss the Council have sustained thereby, and to point out to him that under the Water Works Clauses Acts he was liable to a penilty not exceeding ES. The commit- tee ordered that Mr. Swann report at the next meeting the best means of being in attendance as quickly as pos- sible with the fire appliances in case of fire within the district, of the public being informed where to give warning in case of are, and as to the best means of quickly summoning the fire brigade to a fire. It was also resolved that so much of Ashton-road as is within the district, i e., from thelOak Tree Inn to:the extent of the Authority's boundary, be lighted with gas and that the gas manager lay the necessary mains and street Limps for the purpose; and that Vie Clerk writs to the Haydock Urban District Connell asking them to con- sider the advisability of lighting up so much of Ashton- road as is within their distant. . _ _

_ The Chairman moved, and Mr. McMahon seconded the confirmation of the minutes which were approved. REPORT CF THE MEDICAL OFFICER OF HEAL MI At a meeting of the Highways and Sanitary Com- mittee, the Medical Officer of Health read his report for the quarter ended September 30, which was accepted. Dr. Watkins btated that there were registered : birth., 57 males. 6.3 females, total 120 ; deaths, 33 males. 39 females, total 72 ; excess of births 48. The birth rate was equal to an annual overage of 322 and the death rate 199 per thousand of the estimated population. The infantile death-rate was equal to an annual average of I 298 per cent Tae deaths of children under five years of age were 583 per cent, of the total number. Mo,t ' of these deaths might be reasonably attribated to clima- tic or " seasonable " influences, as in addition to the case" Ecgli!h Cholera" and the 11 cases of diarrhce a, 13 deaths of children were certified as primarily due to Glen-intestinal Catarrh. He was also of opinion that the rain fall, having been much below the average, cvas a factor in the prevalence to such an abnormal extent of intestinal disease. Netwith ttnding all this, eight cases only of infectious disease were not.fied to them only one of them being a child under 5 years of age Six of these cases were removral to the isolation hospi- tal. He must press on the committee's immediate and earnest attention the unreasonable and thereby danger- MTh detention of manure, both animal and vegetable, on the bank of the Sankey Canal,aljoirting Wharf-road,and this in defiance of repeated notices. The stench from it extended over a considerable area, and was so bad that people say "they can taste it w;th their food." This was a positively dangerous nuisance, and it was imperatively necessary thrt the health of the people in the locality shou!d net be secondary to the cenvenience of the owners of the manure. With reference to a dis- infecting chamber referred to by the Medical OFficer rf Health in Ws report for the quarter ended June 30,1898, the sub-committee who were appointed to consider th- question were requested to visit two or three places where disinfecting chambers are in use and again report. UNABATED NUISANCES.

NEW BUILDINGS.

The highways and Sanitary CommittPP approved building plane for Mr. Edwin Molvneux, 8 hone, veargraye-road ; Mr. A. Evett, S. Helene-road, stable, bask Mark-street: Dr. Latharn, Croee lanP, dwellinc house; Mr. R. Eaton, S. HP:ea-road, waehhouse; Eire- town Electric Supply Company, workshop, Graft hi- street.

div.p: TFIE POLLUTION OF NEWTON LAKE. STATEMENT BY THE CFIAIRMAN.

With reference to the pollution of IVl'llingferd Brook, the surveyor and assistant surveyor, acting upon in- structions given at the last meeting, reported that the 12-inch (sewr proposed to b • nonstrinted by Golhorne Urban District Connell would, in their opinion, when completed, prevent the flow of any untreated sewage from any part of their district into Minh:Word Brook. With vgard to Ashton-in-Makerlield, they reported that that Authority had several outlets into the brook, from which apparently un-pur;fied condition, WAS, at sewageatthetimin n eof their visit, Rowing into the brook A letter, eated October 14, was rad from Mevr i.rfonse. man and Company, solicitors to Lori Newton, giving the Council two months' notice, under the Rivers Pollu- tion Prevention Acts, to cease polluting Millingford and Newton Brooks. and Newton Lake, *thin two months, I otherwise legal proceedings would be taken. The Chairman 'aid before putting the motion with re- I ference to poragraphs relating to Newton Lake it was satisfactory to note from the courteous letter from Mem.. Houseman and Company. Lord Newton'a solicc tors, there was a prospect of their taking steps t purify Newton Mere or dam upon which their Medical Officrr of Health so strongly noticed in his report of July last. He (the Chairman) trusted sonything would be done to remove the offensive accumulation which had taken place there for the past 20 years or more. This, accord- ing to statements Made to the Council might become in hot weather a serious danger to public health The Council as the health authority under the Public Health Act bad given watice to Lord Newton's agent to abate this nuisance and doubtlers Messrs. Hue- man would advise meastins being taken to ameliorate the exiiting condition of the bvi of Newton Mere,and thus prevent all porsible ground for the snore. hension that an epidemic might arise in the township owing to neglect within private property be'onging to their client. The Sanitary Committee, he understood, had plans for a new ,IRWRieGI scheme, and when this woe approved of he hoped they would lose no time in bring- ing it before the Council. He was glad to state that the County Council last week resolved to suggest to the Local Government Board a relaxation of their cast-iron rules as to sewage schemes. This, he thought Would he, if accepted, a ;Wolin benefit and facilitate this and many other authorities in Lancashire to promote the public health by adopting efficient arrangements for the treatment of their sewage.

COMPANY.

A letter dated octobe-r-5-t-h;w-a-s -read from the limcbto Sz North-Western Railway Cornuany, stating that th. sewage from a number of cottagei in Common-road is discharged inti their canal. and calling unon the Coun- cil to take steps to prevent the gewage falling into the canal. Whereup'm it was ordered that the Sur reyor report at the nest meeting unon a scheme which would remedy the complaint of the Railway Company and sub- mit an eqtitrate of the cost of such scheme. To say that the news earns as a shc.ck to the family and friends. is to put a mild expression upon it,for such a distressing event was entirely unexpected. A cablegram was reneivei by Mr. Roberts on Saturday afternoon from the Rev. Thomas Newman, St. John', stating that young Mr. Roberts was serioualy ill. His father wired back immediately telling Mr. Newman t. get all the help he pcssibly could. This was some solace r 0 the family, who were satisfl-d that, b.iog with Mr. Newman in St. John's, he would receive the hest :Wen- I tion medically and otherw:se, but it ws thuht that his wif-'s recent illness has been a period of anxiety to him, and he had allowed hirnaelf to run down, until be- yond medical aid. div.head: DEATH OF THE REV. HERBERT MONK, NEWTON.
div.p: DEATH OF THE REV. HERBERT MONK, NEWTON.

A rnost painful sensation was caused during the service at St. Peter's Church, Newton, on Sunday last when at the close of the sermon the Rev. H. Rowla nds,curate, made the announcement that the reeeected vicar, the Rev. EL Monk had passed away after a brief illness. It was known by many or the cengregation that the rev. gentlemen was some- what indi.posed, but there was not the slightest thought that there would ba a fatal termination. and tie result came with a shook all the more sudden He had been in declining health f3r some weeks, but on Sunday October 23rd, he preached the two harvest fe3tival sermons for his nephew, the Rev. Arthur Monk Smith, at Whorlton, near Darlington. He went to Grange on October 24-h, intending to return to Newton rn the following Friday, but as he felt very unwell he returned On the Thursday, and was exceedingly ill in the train on the way home. From that day there was almost complete loss of digestive p3wer. and between then and Friday last he lose eleven pounds in weight, He however, preached at St. Peter's on Sunday October 30th. His health did not improve, and he was attended by Dr. Watkins and Dr. Graham Steele of Manchester,but tneir efforts were of no avail and he sank from sheer exhaustion and passed away quietly on Sunday morning laet,ehortly after 11 o'clock. As soon ae the sad IIeWS became known touching references were made in the vari- -0119 churchee. by the Rey. H. Rowlands. Rev. James Allot% Rev. T. R. Matthews and R IV, qr. Jones of Golborne. His sole surviving sister Mrs. Monk Smith, and her two sons arrived at Newton on Saturday and were thus able to be present at the bed side when the deceased gentlemen exoimd. The late vicar at the time of his death was 62 years of age, having been born on the 22nd October 1836, at Levenshulme, Manchester, where his early school daye were pasted. He studied for the ministry and in 1861 was ordained by the Bishop of Wincheeter and licensed to the curacy of West Cowes. In 1565 he was appointed curate of St. Peters, Ne woe and in 1871 was Appointed vicar and h.:41 the living until his death. His lile was of a quiet descrintion, hut his heart was in his work, and from 1865, no- thing but illness prevented him from being present at every annual vestry meeting. His greatest wish was to see the restoration of St Peters Church com- pleted, and this wish was gratified. A friend writ- ing to Dr Watkins, on Tue•day, stated that qr. Monk was happy in having lived to see the accom- pli4iment of his dearest object in life in Newton, ' namely the rebuilding of St. Peters Chnrch. ITs took an intereit in politics, but not an active Dart, and hie generous treatment of the poor was an at- tribute well known in the parish. The deceased gentleman was never rnar'ted. The living, which is of the gross value of ..£230, is in the gift of Lord Newton.
