div.head: BA.TrLE OF THE ROSES.
div.p: THE BA.TrLE OF THE ROSES.
GREAT MA.TCH AT SALFORD. TIIE V)RK3HIRENIEN TRIUMPHANT.

[BY OUR OWN REPORTER]. Tee year 1893 is a great one for Yorkshiremen. They have whacked us at cricket and they have whacked us at football—in fact the Red Rose seems to hive been trailing in the dust for a long time, while the White Rose has reared its head proudly to the skies. Even insignificant. Cheshire profited by Lancashire's feebleness and climbed up one rung of the county tidier over the broken Red Rose. And now the last heavy blow has fallen. Yorkshire has extinguished Lancashire's Pole remaining chance of regaining her supremacy in Northern Union foetbell. It all happened at Salford—that Royal, but muddy borougb. I went there myself on Saturday ; yes, I actually deserted the town club and went to 809 what the chosen of the County Palatine could d 3 against their Northern neighbours. As things turned out they could do very little. The " grate the" began at three o'clock and out of respect for the occasion, the rain which has of late been very persistent in its endeavovrs to form an additional ocean, ceased work. There was just a parting splash at 2 o'clock, at which the faint-hearted ones shuddered and doffing their top- co its returned to fireside comforts. rho County Committee, in their wisdom, had seen fit to double the prices of admission, a rather questionable policy. True, there were about 12,000 people who paid the d ouble charge, but they none the less felt I somewhat victimised and inclined to jib at a mini- mum of Is. Probably there would have been doub'e the number present if the prices had been more reasonable. It is a bit rough on a football enthusiast to be compelled to wallow through mud' and water in order to reach a turnstile wnere he has to fork out twice as much as u-us!. When I say "wallow" lam perhaps stating the case rather strongly, for there was aaciniered way skirting the edge of the morass which usually does duty for the road to New Barns. As we frequently hear, it is not everyone who can keep to the narrow way, and on Saturday I noticed quite a number of people traversing the broad road, but weetaer from choice or force of circumstances awl cruse, I am unable to say, but I should incline to the belief that choice had little to do with it. These luckless wighte certainly did wallow ; they were up to the eyes in mud —the eyes of their boots of course. Once on the field however, and the condition of things under foot was much bettered.No fault could be fogad with the accommo- dation provided, each and all having a good and uninterrupted view of the game. Punctually to time Archie Rigg led his burly fifteen into the en- clo,ure amid hearty welceming cheers. Tee visitors looked every bit the smart lot they proved, with their white jerseys and dark blue pants. Oae might havepresaged Lancashire's defeat immediately they appeared on the scene, such a neglected, un- washed, and forgotten appearance they presented Last year's jerseys apparently did service in CJlll- pany with nether garments hailing from here,there, and everywhere. They looked a shabby lot—really second hand—and it was difficult to feel any thrill of pride in the fifteen ushered into the arena by George Messenger. I do hate a team to appear slovenly and uncarel for. At times it is pardonable in a town club, but in the county's representatives never. And worst of all the Red Rose champions played as they looked. I suppose I might as well give the names of the players and officials representing the coinages. Here they are then : Lane ishire : R Bety (Widnes), back ; J Hoskins (Salford). right wing, T Williams (Salford), right (centre, 0 Badger (Swinton), left centre), and D Traynor (St. Helens), left wineahreequarter backs; G olessenger (captain) (Broughton Rangers), and Nelson (Broughton Rang ers),half backs; J aftearthy (Wigan), G Whitehead (Broughton Rangers), J Evans (Swinton). P Taylor (Leigh). 0 Heslop (Widnes), W Briers (St. Helens), J Williams (Sal- ford), and J Harrison (Rochdale Hornets), for- wards. Tarkshire.—J Metcalfe (Wakefield), back; J Lumley (Leeds), left wing, J 13 Parker (Bramley), left centre. A 0 Goldthorpe (flunslet), right centre, and F W Cooper (Bradford), right wing, three- quarter backs : A. Rigg (Halifax) (captain), and 11391)in:son (Hensler.), half-backs; A Kemp (Hull Kingston Rovers), A Starks (Hull Kingston Rovers) W Oils (Hull), T Wilkinson Of anningham), T Broadley (Bradford). Chambers (Huddersfield), J Gath (Batley), and .T Remege (Hunslet), forwards. Touch-judges: J H Smith (Widnes) ant H H Waller (Brighouse Rangers). Referee: J Bruck- haw (Stockport and Cheshire Union). For a quarter-of-an-hour the Lancashire men looked as if they were going to belie their appearance and uphold their reputation. During that time two tries were obtained, one by Hoskins, and the other by Traynor. Both were the result of clever combination by the backs, floekins rushing over after Williams hid run splendidly and male a beautiful opening. Tray- , nor's try cams from a long pass by Badger, the sturdy St. Helens man having no difficulty in beat- ing the Yorkshire backs near the corner. Both goal kicks failed, but nevertheless the home repre- sentatives felt on decidedly good terms with them- selves. But, alas, the Lancastrians hat only flat- tered to deceive. fhe blood of the Tykes was now roused, and by dint of sterling forward play they closely inve,ted the home goal. A scrimmage on the Lancashire line gave Archie Raw his first op- portunity and the dashing Yorkshire captain eluded NI- gauger and Nels on, and scored a try near thel posts. Cooper took the place kick and lifted his side to within a point of their opponents with a neat.goal. Now it was Lancashire's turn to be roused, ant the Red Rose representatives quickly raced to the opposite end. What chance there was here was spoiled through the slowness of the men behind the scrimmage. Rigg secured, and by a short punt and quick follow up called on Batey to make a grand save. The homesters were again hard pressed, and son found themselves in a minority. The irrepressible Rigg ran round the pack, and at the correct moment threw to Robinson who raced over like a streak of lightning. Cooper obliged with another fine goal. Lancashire now awoke to the fact that they must put in all they knew if they were once mere going to be on the safe side. The Tykes seemed of the same opinion, and for a brief spell nlay of the deadliest description ensued at half-way. Yorkshire's grand front rank claimed possession of the bell oftener than not, and ere long Robinson broke away, threw to Goldthorpe who ran we before transferring to Broadley. and the burly Bradford captain rushed over with he energy of a steam-engine. Badger triei to stop him but it was useless. Again was Cooper called upon, and once more did he pilot the oval between the sticks. Before the interval Gold- thorpe took a penalty near mid-field and dropped at goal, the ball hitting the upright and bounding back into play—herd luck for Yorkshire's champion droppist. At half-time the Lancashire pulse Was feebly but plockily, and the teams crossed ob:tlng lerwith the score 15 points to 6 points in favour of Yorkshire. Both quarters had been lively, but the latter especially so. Lancashire were not long in putting en six pointe.but once the Tykes started to retaliate and they rubbed it in without mercy. The way in which they put, 15 points together was an eye- opener to the crowd, and well-nigh crushing to the home team. -

Lancashire started their almost hopelesa task of regailing lest ground with a man short. M'Carthy, of Wigan. hdrl sustained an injury to his shoulder which necessitated his exchanging the field for the hospital. The men of the White Rose were soon on tie attack. T. Williams rendered good ser- vice with a c:ever run and kick, but the relief afforde.d was only momr-ntary. Though still defending the Lancashire men showed a dogged determination which was an omen that they were far from eone with. Batey had an unsuccessful shot at goal from centre, and the ball was quickly pawed hack. Loose play gave the Yorkshire for- :Nerds an opportunity of displaying their abilities in the Open, and starting with a dribble they coin- PletolY beat the Lancashire hacks, Kemp ultimately Picking up and running over with try number four. Cooper this time hada more difficult angle to nego- tiate, hut without any apparent difficulty he sent the ball plumb through the centre again. A last effort to nut themselves on a better foeting was made by Lancashire, and they were aided by Wil- kinson having to retire from the Yorkshire ranks with a swelled heed—not from conceit but from concussion. Yorkshire were penned under their eoa', and 'AlesQenger obtaining the ball male good use of it. Williams received the pass and aft,r making headway handed to his club-mate, Hoskins. who registered Lancashire's third try at the corner. There were cheers of joy, and hope almost, r Traynor had the difficult task of shooting at goal alloted to him, and he made a grand though unsuccessful attempt. Play was both even and exciting after this, Cooper had a goal kick

div.head: REFLECTIONS.
div.p: REFLECTIONS.

That the best team won there can be no doubt. Yorkshire's superiority was very marked, after the first quarter of an hour, and though they only crossed the goal-line four times to their opponents three times, the score of LO points to 9 is a pretty fair indication of the play. I was very mace sur- prised at the poor show made by the Red Rose, not- withstanding the fact that there were several changes in the team originally selected. Apart from their lack of method, the Lancastrians seemed Ito have nothing of the "go " and dash which characterised the pay of their foes. The Tykes played by far the hardest, most determined game, never seeming to tire or give the homesters a moment's respite. Lancashire did at times perform worthily—all the tries were the outcome of COOl- - efforts—but taken generally they gave a feeble exhibition. It was principally at half-back where they were let down. How the many Warringtonians present must have sighed for Bate'e resource and skill ! I know I did frequently. Messenger and Nelson were terribly slow. There is some excuse for them in the fact that the Tykes had the best of the argu- ment forward, but all the same there were plenty of opportunities for a couple of smart halves to shine. Comparing the two pecks, the palm must be given to the visiting eight. Indeed the " Yarkshire ferwuds," as a heathen from the neighbourhood of Halifax called them, were a grand set. They were strong, fast, and clever in the open, and I don't think a more capable lot ever represented the White Rose. Klieg and Robinsou performed wonders at half back, and those who remember the Halifax cs.3tain's play at Warrington in the cup-tie two years ago will have some idea of his play last Saturday. Robinson was quite as good. In the three-quarter line the Yorketuremen were represen- ted by a safe quartette. Tney were not over brilli- ant, and certainly not superior to the Laucaetire four, who were resp3nsible for the whole of the points secured by the Red Rose. A word of praise should be given to Fred Cooper for his grand goal-kicking. Out of five attempts he landed four goals, and the fifth was charged down when well on the right way. At full-back Metcelfe compared poorly with his vie a vie Batey. ' The Widnes man was seen at his best, and the ser- vice be rendered the defeated side was incalculable.l A finer exhibition of full-back play was never given under such tryingecircumstances I am sure Badger was the failure of the Lancashire three- quarter line, and for a Welsh international his dis- play was heartrending. It was through him that Traynor got so few opportunities to show the sterl- ing stuff of which he is made. The famous Sal- ford pair, Hoskins and Williams, gave every satis- faction on the right wing, their combined play being very effective. The Lancashire forwards though beaten, played a plucky game, Whitehead (of Broughton) beim; the shining light. The game itself was a very interesting one, full of excitement and contested in the best spirit. Yorkshire deserved Ito win, and no one who saw the encounter will be- grudge them the County Championship for 1893-9.

div.head: RITUALISTIC CONTROVERSY AT HA YDOCK.
div.p: THE RITUALISTIC CONTROVERSY AT HA YDOCK.
EXTRAORDINARY SUNDAY MORNING INCIDENT. A WORSHIPPER REILIOVED BY THE POLICE.

Ritualistic controversy that has beers going on in connection with Haydock Church for about a year com.., - to a crids on Sunday morning, when Mr. Jossph Hilton, who at the last of the series of unsatisfactory vestry meetings held this year was proposed as the parishioners warden, was removed frcin the church by the Police on a c'sarge of brawling. Mi. Hilton is an extreme mem- ber of the Church Association. He lives at Ashton-in- Makerfield, about two miles from Haydock Church, but has recently commenced to attrnal Haydock Church and take part in the agita,tion that has been carried on against the proceelinas of the Rev. Francis Ireland, vicar. Oa Sunday morning while Mr. Ireland was preaching on the Holy Communion, Mr. Hilton stood up and said that the doltrine Mr. Ireland was expound- ing was contrary to the Thirty-first Article of tne Prayer Book. The vicar then stopped his sermon and sent Mr. Cunliffe, his warden, for the police, and Mr. Hilton walked out of the churth alone with Insplctor Scott and another officer. It is understood that a summons will be applied for.

(N.S.) No calls to be made at any port or ports other than those mentioned. The vws,ls employed to he specially adapted end fitted therefor. Each vessel with 8,500 to dead weight capacity, and capable when fully laden, el steaming 12 knot e per hour with deckage accommodaton for cattle. Ths service is to be a fortnightly one, sailing from each of the terminal poiti ar rey,ular intervals of 14 d ivs.• The subsidy to be given is fix2d at the rate of £B,OOO per annum.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

HILL CLIFFPI AND STOCIMN HEATH UNITED BAND OF Hoes.—The monthly entertainment in connection with. the above was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom on Mon- day night and there was an overflowing congregation. The president,Rev.J.S.Fluehea was in the chair and ex- orAssed his pleasere at the larva attendance and the act iva irtsrest manifested. The Chairman was supported hp the secretary Mr. George Whiteflold. Mr. Dunn, and Mr. A. B. Kenworther the organist. There were two anecial attractions for this meeting: Mr. J. H. Hutchins the day school temperance lecturer, belonging to the Lancashire and Cheshire Union of Bands of Hoes was ring tn be present and give one of his experimental addresses, and there :•Fts to be a party of friends from Sankey Bridges. Mr. Hutchins gave a capital and clear address on the influence of alcohol on the blood, which I was illustrated by diagrams and experiments. The party from Sankey Bridges rendered very good service. The Miggf4q Woolley, Cerradine and Jackson, sane very wed, and Miss Alice Worrell gave a pathetic recitation in an effective manner. Misses Drum, Sudlow, Brough,John- eon, Cotterill and Hardy, gave a dialogue in good style. Recitations were also given by Misses Tevlor, Dorothy Martin, Lilly Percival, Mice Taylor, and Martar George Arthur Whltleld and Harold Moores, whilst Edith Houghton. sang very sweetly the solo " Ah 'Us the old old story." Toe programms was an exceptionally good one and greatly appreciated. It was a pity that the room was not large enough to aecommodate all who de- sired to be presook. Warm thank., were given to the en- tertainers and another successful meeting FM brought tea close.
SPIRITUALIST MRRTINGS.

At the meetings of the Spiritualist Society on Sunday and Monday, Miss Jones, of Liverpool, was the speaker. tier address on Sunday evening was upon "The Dawn of Day," in which she referred to the unrest and uncertainty in the theological world. There were good audiences and at each meeting Miss Jones gave a number of clairvoyant and pyschometric &lineations, many of which were admitted to be correct. div.head: NOTES ON GAAES AND ATHLETICS. •
div.p: NOTES ON GAAES AND ATHLETICS. •
RUGBY FOOTBALL.

Though I did not exactly predict it! hinted at the possibility of Warrington finding Millom too hard a nu', to crack, even though the Cumberland club is only in the second division. Several clubs in the Lancashire League have had the fact impressed upon thom very forcibly that there are teams who know a little about football outside the first division. And now it is War- rington's turn. Millons triumphed by 3 tries to nothing.

The defeat is not a circumstance I attach much irn- portance to, and neel not alarm people who view the match thie Satur:lay with Broughton Ringers apprehen- sively. The Warrington team without its capable captain is like a ship without a rudder, and can bardly be expected to steer tb straight course to victory. Then again the players were by no means inclined to kill themselves with exertion solely for the purpose of win- ning an unimportant friendly match. Their energies will all be required in the nexC two league mat:thee. Con- sequently the Mill= men did not find their task excep- tionally difficult, though they were lucky to keep War- rington from scoring on several occasions. We cannot begrudge them the win, and it lifts the Millotnites into the seventh heaven of delight. On Good Friday they may be awakened to the fact that they are not quite as ' good as they think. Wilderspool is a harder place to defeat the Wirepullers at than the Cumberland town.

All the points Alillom scored were obtainwl by J. Young,a speedy wing threequarter who faced Fish. me home team worked to him very effectively and he made good use of his opportunities. I see that he is selected to play for Cumberland county against Cheshire at Run- corn, and he deserves his olace.

Warrington were rather let down at half hack. Neither Aahurst nor R.Bate is particularly brilliant when not un- der the lea lership of" Smack," and they found North.. more and Wharton rather too much for them. Fish was the most prominent man among the backs for Warring- ton, and had the hardest of luck in not getting a couple of tries. Isherwood did good service in the centre, espe- cially on the defence. Hallam was in excellent form and replied with interest to the Cumberland men'a long punts.

Robbed of all interest by th—obir ame at Salfor 3. th 7 three matches played in the Lancashire Senior Competi- tion of the Northern Union were net without surprises. At St. Helens the representatives of Loigh took the " glass" men down to the tune of eight points to none. True, the home team was shor. of Brier and Traynor, but that hardly accounts for such a beating. Stockport, as nauchto the surprise of their own supporters as any- one else, managed to beat Tyldesley by saven points to none. Since tne success of the Stockport men in the Cheshire V. Lancashire match they seamed to have regained some of theirreal form. Runcorn admini.te!ed the customary beating to Morecambe, the sore being thirteen points to three.
The results of matches up to date,and the positions of rho clubs in the Lancashire Comp3tition ans as follow :

The County match between Laneashire and Yoeces`iire with which I have deal: at len,th in another co'unin proved disastrous to the County Palatine. Unless they can give the Cumberland men a licking Lancashire will have the unenviable woolen spoon in their poessesion. Their display at Salford does not promise very well even ,for the match with Cumberland, as the men of the north have had their ranks reinforced by the new clubs whe have recently gone over to the Nsrthern Union. Seaton, Millom, and Marypor: provide men whose capa- bilities are not to be sneered at. The result of their match with Cheshire at Runcorn will be looked upon with interest in Lancashire.

A great deal of excitement is being shown owing to Warrington's encounter with Broughton Rangers at Wilderspool. The Rangers have been going very strongly this season, and have only one defeat recorded azainst them, and this at the hands of Sailor 1. Still I have an idea that they will meet their match at Warrington. I The local lads are determined to take the burly Rangers down. They have done it tr,fore—when the Broughton men were quite as powerful—and they lean dolt again if they play for all they are worth. At half-back War- rington ought to have an advantage. Messenger and NP!- son appear to have lost the art of quick passing alto- gether.

The " A "team 'accomplished an excellent perform- ance against Loatock Gralam on Saturday, as the seore of 24 points to 6 clearly shews. Fish's old club mates played a good game but they were not smart enough for the "A" team that is going to win the championship. Harris, late of Latchford Rangers, played a wonderfully good game, and the three tries he obtained would have done credit to any rean. If he keep; un his dash and cleverness it will nct be long before he figures in better company.

The Saints had Runcorn Wes as visitors on Saturday and the rssult was a win for thn hninn tni.nii by 3 tries to mi. There was not much tn chnse V`P'rx,en the teams in the Arst half, but in te second filf the St. Marys showed their supr(macy and scored three tries. The passing and tackling of the winners was vary good and showed a great improvement on nrovinns matches. CIA

PERSONAL.
The Rev. F. H.Wales curate at Daresbury Church will shortly leave the district and commence duties atlHoylake. ELECTION EXPENSES
The expenses of Mr. William Furness, the Libera candidate for St. John's ward in the recent munici- pal elections, have been returned at .£3l 18s. 6d. Y M.C.A. FRIARS' GREEN.

On Monday evening in the Lecture Hall, a lan- tern lecture, entitled " Here and there with a Camera' was given by Mr. R. H. Fisher. general secretary of the North Liverpool ILM CA. He showed a series of beautiful photographic pictures. taken during his rambles through England and Wales. The audience showed special appreciation of views which Mr. Fisher bad been able to obtain in and around Hawarden Castle. Mr. W. Hickman kindly acted as chairman. A BRAVE RESCUE.

On Saturday. hit. David Meldrum. manager, pre- sented a constable named Fred McPherson, in the employ of the Cheshire Lines Committee with a gold medal, in recognition of his bravery in rescuing a man from being killed at the Warrington Central Station. It appears that an Irish farm labourer, finding he was on the wrong platform attempted to cross the line in front of an approach- ing express train, but fell in doing so, and McPher- son on seeing this immediately jumped on the line and just succeeded in dragging the man clear as the train passed the spot. YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.

Being open Sunday, the lecture Hall was crowded last Sunday afternoon on the occasion of the P.S.A. meeting. Mr. James Shaw presided. Mr. R. H. Pearson skilfully rendered two violin solos, and Miss Pie Mouse gave a capital rendering of " The Distant Shore" The Rev. FE. . Roberts gave an excellent address on " Moral greatness" and Mes-rs. R. Wood, G. Efolford, G. B. ifolford, and F. Hickman also look part in the meeting, which was of a very pleasant. and profitable character. GOOD TNIIPLARY.

• The weekly meeting of the Temperance Mission Lodge of the I O.G T , was held on Wednesday in the Temperance Hall, Academy-street. Brother Roberts, P.C.T., presided over a large attendance of members and visitors from Earleetown, St. Helens and Stockton Beath. Two candidates were admitted into the Order by initiation and one by re-obliga- tion. After the usual business Sad been transacted, Sister Sheath celebrated her 29th anniversary of Good Temolary by giving a supper to all present. Brother Woods, Earlestown, Brother Taylor, C.C.T., Earlestown, Brother Francis, C C., St. Helens and Sister Woods, C.S.J.T., Earlestown, delivered short addresses,congratulating Sister Sheath on the event. Brother J. Sheath responded on behalf of Sister Sheath. The following programme was then ren- dered :—Sister sheath, recitation ; Sister Nurse, song ; Sister Millington, song; Brother Nurse, song. The meeting was then dlosei after an enjoyable and profitable evening pan neen spent.

At the Manchester Assizes on Toursiay mornin2th Grand Jury returned a true bill against Emma Jan.? North, 27, a servant of Blackpool, who is charged wit° the murder of her newly-born female child between tha„ 27th and 30th August last. div.p: MATCH.

A youth named James Partington (19), of 85, St. GeV man-street, Farnworth, has just sun mmbed to injuried received whilst playing football on Saturday. Deceased was taking part in a match between St. Mar?'s Parks Walkden, and Hawshaw-lane, at Tottington, when tid collided with an opponent, whose knee struck him witll great force in the abdomen. He died from the injuried on Wednesday. FATAL RESULT OF BOXING. Torn Turner, who was injured at the National Sport, ing Club on Monday, died on Thursday afternoon St Charing Cross Hospital. Turner was unconscious right up to the time of deatb. His mother and the young woman he was soon to marl were present.

Four negroes were lynched, six men were killed, and' four mortally injured in election frays in Texas. SAD DEATH OF A MAGISTRATE. FALLING ON THE FIRE. Alderman E. T. 889, of Lydd, Kent, met with a elq, accident on Wednesday, which has since ternainate° f atally. Efe had been in indifferent health for sornd drag past, but he attended proceedings in connection with 06 election of the Mayor. It appears, however, that uPeri returning home, and whilst standing with his back the mantelpiece he slipped and fell on the fire. No otle was in the room at the time, and he was unable to ge! up again, but he managed to reach the boll. Assistaneff was soon at hand, but by this time his clothes were e.." alight, and he was partially burnt oa the back and kW, Medical ail was summoned, but he expired at three o'clock on Thursday morning from the effect of burlil and shock. He was a member of the Corporation for 44 years, and was several times Mayor.

EXPLOSION AT A. WARRINGTON CHEMIST'S SHoP. AN ASSISTANT SEVERELY BURNED: On Friday afternoan at ten minutes past two an alarming accident occurred at the shop of Mr. Charles J. Chamberlain, chemist, 66, Church-strret. It seems that an assistant, named Harold Wiggingt in, 20 years of age, was mixing some harness paste, and was using turpentire.when he upset a gas stove, and an explosion occurred. Other chemicals in bittles also exploded,blow• log out the side wind )ao in Orchard-street. Wiggington was shockingly burned about the face neck and arms. After the explosion the unfortunate young man, suc- ceeded in groping his way out of the shop, and was taken to the Marquis of Granby public-house where the usual remedies wore applied by Mr. William Whittle until the arrival of a can. It was evident that he was in great pain. The frint part of the shop was soon in a blaze, and pending the arrival of the fire brigade, for which a message had been despatched, assistance was rendered by a number of hands from 13rundrett's brewery. Mr. William Bramhall, employed by Mrs.Brun- drett playing on the flames with a small fire extin- guisher. When the fire brigade arrived, with one of the steam fire engines, Superintendent Turner found that there was little or nothing for him and his men to do. The interior of the shop presented a very black and dis- mal appearance. Not only were the windows broken and hundreds of bottles smashed,but the woodwork was considerably damaged,and the loss is put down at about £2OO. It was rumoured that Mrs. Charnbirlaiii, who is in a delicate state of health, was in one of the hdrooms upstairs, and Inspector Phillips, who was in charge of the plice, dir mted one of his men to brea't open one of the windows at the back. Hi did so, hut it was found th ,t the lady was saf in anoth.r part of the house. Much sympathy is felt for Mr. Chamberlain, not only with regard to the injuries to his as dstant,but also of ith regard to the loss he has sustained in his business
